utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Mr. Ackerman and good morning to you too. So we will be hearing the testimony of Lord Ashdown this morning. Do you have anyone -- any other witness, too, because I'm informed that at least my secretary prepared me the documents of another witness too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I anticipate that Lord Ashdown will probably take if not the whole of today's session, a goodly part of it and though there is another witness here, I'm not at the moment given any instructions for him to be brought over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour I want to deal at the end but I'm anxious that Lord Ashdown should be able to get through his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have a number of witness problems for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if I can deal with that at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will discuss the situation, just mark time and we'll adjust accordingly. See how much time you require and if in the meantime during the break, you think you could perhaps solve some of the problems or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour it's not a soluble problem with the Defence. It's a problem of getting witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. So let's bring in Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that you are already familiar with the procedure here. So I ask the usher to hand over to you the text of the solemn declaration that you're required to enter to make before you start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and Ms. Korner will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown will you be kind enough to give the Court please your full name?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: My name is Jeremy John Durham Ashdown and I'm frequently and most usually known as Paddy Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very briefly dealing with as it were your biography, I think that you were a member of the army for some years, subsequently a diplomat, member of parliament, eventually becoming leader of the Liberal Democrat party in Great Britain, then being made a member of the House of Lords and I think currently High Representative for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Lord Ashdown, as you know, what I would like to ask you about today is a trip that you made to Bosnia in August of 1992, and in particular, in relation to your visit to two camps. I think it's right that throughout this period, you kept a diary?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, can you tell us was it written by you by hand or typed up by you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: My normal practice and it's certainly the practice that I've followed in respect of the entries which we shall be referring to, was to dictate the night of the events, every night, I dictated my diary in detail. There are some elements of my diary where less important, less interesting things are happening where I might dictate the following day but my normal practices especially in -- during events -- during days when I believe the events would be important to me in the future, I would dictate that night. So these diaries would have been dictated into a dictating machine that night, subsequently sent to my secretary in Yeovil in Somerset who would type them up and the copies then would be placed in the bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think you provided to the Prosecution and have got with you photocopies of the relevant pages, relevant to this particular trip, to Bosnia, the 8th through to the 11th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's correct. It would perhaps be helpful to the Court if I were to point out that in respect of these entries which were amongst I believe the most important category of entries to my diary, for these type of entries which would include not just events such as this but for instance meetings with the Prime Minister, meetings with the President, I would then ask my secretary as soon as the pages were typed up to resubmit them to me. I would read them through and make manuscript amendments which is the manuscript amendments that you see here which would therefore have been made within a week or ten days of the diaries being actually dictated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you've got copies yourself but Your Honour could I ask that they formally be made an exhibit in this case? That would be Exhibit P1534. And I think Your Honours were provided with copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we deal with the detail of the events, could you just tell us how did you come to make this visit to Bosnia in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well it sprang out of the first visit that I made I have to say almost my happen stance to Sarajevo in July of this year. Ms. Korner this was a period after the British election when there is not much going on and I have to say I knew very little indeed in fact I knew nothing about Yugoslavia as it then was but a colleague recommended to me that as we drew close to the summer recess, that this was going to be a big issue and that I should go and take a look for myself. So in July of, late July of 1992, I first went to Croatia and then flew into Sarajevo and spent sometime in the city. Obviously at that time that event got a good deal of press coverage because there weren't many other people going into Sarajevo at the time and I argued the case on the press as I saw it from inside the siege of Sarajevo, and then I came home and my wife and I were intending to take two weeks holiday. We were in fact in France on the first day of our holiday and I received a message from my office that Radovan Karadzic had said that since I had seen quotes the Muslim point of view, close inverse commas, I should come to see his point of view, the Serb point of view. I consulted with my office about this time the first press reports were appearing in relation to the atrocities at Omarska and Keraterm, and so I agreed with my colleague, sir Russell Johnston who was at this stage, one of our foreign affairs spokesmen that we would make the trip together. But the condition that I put to Mr. Karadzic was that if we were to go on this trip we would have full and free access to wherever we wished to go, making it clear that we would wish to go and have a look at some of the camps which were then being exposed by the press. It was our original intention to take somebody from the Red Cross with us but the Red Cross for reasons which are entirely appropriate decided that the link to any particular side would be a political connection they would not wish to have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down because of the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Karadzic's invitation on I think I've got the date right, the 8th of August I left my wife in France and went to Budapest where I met Sir Russell Johnston. We drove over land to Belgrade because of course the sanctions were then in place. We had meetings with the Yugoslav leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, I'm so sorry, I wonder if you could just slow down slightly please because the interpreters are having a problem?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think in fact they've missed part of his testimony which probably ought to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 6, line ten it looks like there is a part left out. I'm not sure about that but I think it might have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we -- I tell you what I want to come back to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not important any way I know which point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this, before you began the trip you've spoken of the revelation of the camps. Had you actually seen the television footage of Omarska before you went?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner I really can't recall. I had certainly -- I -- it was sufficiently in the front of my mind as an image and as an issue that I suspect I must have seen them or at least seen the still photographs of it. I can't believe that this would have been such an issue for me if I'd simply read a press report but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we are going to hear about your visit to the camp called Manjaca. Had you heard about Manjaca before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Not at this stage. It was our intention to visit Omarska, visit Keraterm, see things for ourselves and visit any other similar camps but at this stage, the word Manjaca hadn't -- I'd never heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you were starting to tell us, I think you began your trip by going to Hungary and then to Belgrade. I think the only part of that -- of that entry in your diary on the 8th of August, when you arrived in Belgrade, did you meet a journalist and we see that at the end of your entry for Saturday, the 8th, and was that Ed Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It was -- it's misspelled in the manuscript amendment that I put in here. It's Ed Vulliamy -- Vulliamy. V-U-L-L-I-A-M-Y, perhaps, he wrote a book subsequently and if I recall at this stage was writing for the Guardian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we move then, please, to the next day, the 9th, Sunday, the 9th of August? I think it's right that from Belgrade, you travelled to Pale or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I travelled to -- from Belgrade we travelled by helicopter to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you there have a meeting with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look I think the third page of your entry for the 9th, you will find?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I don't need to look at the entry. This carries the detail to know that I had an extensive meeting with Radovan Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And during the course of that meeting with Karadzic, did he agree that you could inspect the various camps?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: He first of all took me to a what I can only describe as a show camp on the Serb side of the outskirts of Sarajevo near Lukavica camp. I was immediately suspicious that this was a show camp because of a number of things, including the way the prisoners were behaving. But also the fact that he tried to get me to present some freedom certificates to the prisoners which was manifestly a press stunt to get me involved, and I refused to do this. I said that I was not satisfied, I recall I said that I was not satisfied that this was indeed the kind of conditions that most prisoners were being held in and reminded him of the undertaking which he had given in writing through Mr. John Kennedy, his chief spokesman in the U.K., that I could go anywhere and therefore said to him that it was my intention to go to Banja Luka on the following day, and I particularly wanted to look at camps in the area of Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we then move, please, to the 10th of August, the Monday, and where you I think were driven to Banja Luka and gave a description of the drive. But could you come to the third, the fourth paragraph on that entry? You stated that you frequently passed through areas where the war had just been, with shot-up houses and a lot of torched houses in ethnically mixed areas close to Banja Luka. Can I just ask, how did you know they were ethnically mixed, were you told that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I had taken the trouble to discover before we went which of the villages in these areas we are dealing largely with what is now known as the Posavina corridor were ethnicity mixed. The most glaring example of course was Brcko. We drove through Brcko in which I can't remember the population mixes but there were substantial elements of population from all sides. In fact I knew before I went and the devastation there was very obvious to the eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we come, please, to your description of the army in the next paragraph that you saw? Close to Banja Luka, you described the tanks and the soldiers and then said -- you stated, "I was especially struck by the military bearing of most of the soldiers that I saw. I had expected a ragtag and bobtail gorilla army but they have well disciplined, well turned out and do their job with efficiency. Any idea that the Serb soldiers are not under proper command and control is nonsense." When you say any idea that Serb soldiers are not under proper command and control, was that something that was being said to you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. I have some military experience I was 13 years in the royal marines including in a number of active service theatres. So I think I can recognise a professional soldier when I see one but all the signs were very evident and I remember being struck by the stark contrast between the what Karadzic would have called the Muslim forces, what I think is a more proper name the Bosniak forces in Sarajevo who were very much a civilian army raised at the last moment inadequately equipped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm so sorry, Your Honour, uniforms of varying types, some no uniforms at all, classically no wireless communications equipment. Now the road blocks even the smallest road blocks that we saw on the way around were disposed in a professional military manner with appropriate sightings of fox holes, et cetera. The soldiers were well turned out, all in the same uniform, their uniform, especially the leather items which are difficult to keep up in the field were clean, well maintained, shiny, but in particular I don't recall passing through a single checkpoint that was not equipped with communications equipment and that they were conducting these in a professional manner in constant communication with their headquarters. What of course we subsequently know is that the vast proportion of the old Yugoslav national army were of course taken over by the Republic of Serbs and what we were seeing was the ex-Yugoslav national army one of the best equipped most effective, best coordinated Warsaw Pact armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now when you got to Banja Luka, I think that you then engaged, as you put it, in a war of nerves with the local military. At that stage, did you know about the military camp of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I cannot remember exactly when I got to hear of Manjaca. I think it may have been the previous night when I was at Pale but certainly by this time, I was very conscious that there was one camp that had large camp which people were talking about that had not been visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: And I heard about that obviously from the press. They were saying we must get into Manjaca. We have been into Keraterm and Trnopolje but we hear there are bad thing going on at this camp and we need to get in and take a look. So in these circumstances the press are as much a friend and your lever and instrument as anything else and I agreed that we would combine forces to see if we could build on the promise that Karadzic had made to me to be able to go anywhere and we decided that we would settle on seeking to go to Manjaca. Because that was still a black hole that no one had seen into.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you described in your diary negotiations that you had to undertake to get to see this camp. You don't record any names in your diary. I don't expect you to. But do you remember the names of any of the people that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I regret I don't. Yugoslavia was somewhere which whose geography I was only just coming to terms with and certainly it's language and names is something which was very unfamiliar to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Eventually then you were driven to Manjaca and at that stage was there also a television crew from CNN with you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Ms. Korner I should explain that the first attempts, the first response to my questions about whether we would -- should go in were met with blank refusal from the senior military people in Banja Luka who I record in my diary as being generals. They said if we went in, we would be shot, and that there was a curfew. I seem to recall the standoff went on for probably two hours. I remember noting in my diary and thinking at the time that this may well have been in order to delay our departure so there was time to clean up the camp a bit but in the end, I said that if they were going to shoot us they would have to shoot us in front of the television cameras and that would not only spoil my afternoon but would not do them very much good in the international community and therefore we would go and that at this stage they conceded so yes there were television cameras with us. I think there were -- I cannot remember precisely, sorry, I cannot remember precisely how many but certainly two to my recollection and quite a large number of newspaper journalists as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before we come on to the conversations that you had and what you saw in the camp, can I ask you this? When you went there, did you have any preconceived ideas of what you were going to find or what you expected to find?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, I expected Belsen in a word. I mean by that time my entire perception of what was going on was conditioned by the photographs and pictures which by now I knew I had seen of Keraterm and Omarska of the horrors that were going on there. And of the fact that they were, by any standards, camps whose system practice and intention were to my mind extermination. Either extermination directly or extermination of spirit through brutality and horror of an order which has not been seen on the mainland of Europe since the days of the Second World War. That was the mental condition in which I went into Manjaca. It was what I expected to see, it was what I feared seeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we then look, please, at how you described that visit to Manjaca? You stated that - and we'll have a look at the video that was made by CNN in a moment - but you stated that "Having got entry, you were taken to a briefing room where the camp commandant who is clearly a very frightened man brought in from the front rather bluff and simple soldier, started shouting to us." What led to you record that he was a very frightened man?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you remember?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: He was obviously extremely nervous about your visit. And he adopted immediately a highly aggressive attitude and I recall being subjected to what in memory seems like 20 minutes, maybe half an hour, of shouted propaganda. I drew the conclusion that this was not a man used to running prison camps. I may be wrong. I drew the conclusion that this was a probably a combat soldier brought in to do a difficult job. He, as I recall, produced the Geneva Convention but at the time I remember being told that that was the first time that the Geneva Convention had been seen in the camp. And both then and subsequently, I drew the conclusion that either he had been moved in or he had recently received specific orders to take those from Manjaca and Omarska who I was subsequently to see and care for them would be the wrong word, and ensure that the horrors of Omarska and Keraterm did not continue on the scale that had been seen and observed by the press in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we deal with the your diary entry, you state after you mention the Geneva Conventions that he showed you, and you say you asked him one or two questions, all of which he took to be hostile and chiefly, you say, "I wanted to know where the front line interrogation unit for the soldiers was." And he had to eventually admit there was one.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, there wasn't one. That should read, I apologise, it does read there was one but there wasn't one. What I was seeking to establish here is were these soldiers? Were we dealing with people who were prisoners of war, which is what he claimed or were we dealing with civilians rounded up and incarcerated and I concluded that it was the latter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all people who were soldiers or that they -- did he admit that these were civilians?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: To be honest, ten years distance I can't recall precisely but I asked him the specific question and I recall that his answer was something like, "These are all people who are a threat to the security of our state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen the -- I've seen it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Korner and Lord Ashdown, I've been asked by the interpreters to ask you to allow a very short interval between question and answer. Okay? Thanks. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we -- when you went round the camp, did you ask to see the people who had come from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes indeed. They were my first priority. I had heard that some 1.000, 2.000 people had been moved from Omarska a matter of days before. Indeed, if I recall, the commandant told me that, that he had been asked to take in these people. So I asked immediately to see them. As I recall the event, they tried to take us to other prisoner incarceration areas where people had been in Manjaca longer but I insisted ongoing to see the people who had come from Omarska and Keraterm, and after a little confrontation, that was agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the simplest thing at this stage before we go back to, Your Honour, is to have a look at the video that was made of at least part of your visit to the camp. It's already been handed to the video -- the audiovisual unit and it's P468. So if the usher could put the thing on to the video and if that could be played?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we are going to come into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. We have had now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we pause the video there, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, the commentator said that you were allowed to speak to the men privately. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That is correct. Again, if I recall, we had something of a confrontation to start with I was taken in there and given the opportunity of speaking to them but with the commandant there, and with the -- with the guards there. So I asked that the commandant and the guards should go. And there was a disputation about this but eventually they agreed they would. And as I recall, kept one television camera behind with an agreement from the journalist that if -- if I did not wish to do -- that the footage that was taken during these private interviews should be shown they would not be shown. In other words I had a complete control over the use of that footage. I naturally didn't want to get a position where somebody would be telling me something which would then be broadcast and put their lives at risk. And the private conversations which then ensued certainly had a considerable bearing on the judgement that I made in this all-too-brief visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it was that they said to you which led you to the judgement that you made?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, they said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can a break please be made between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... food, they dreaded the winter, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault again, the interpreters are asking for the break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's my fault entirely.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: They said to me that conditions are very hard, the food was inadequate. Medical coverage was sparse or non-existent. They greatly feared the winter because they were sleeping in the open on the, as I recall it, earth floor, but that things were much better here than they had been at Omarska. They were not being killed in large numbers. They were not being killed. And they were suffering harsh, even brutal treatment but that they were not being tortured. The overwhelming impression, Ms. Korner, that I got was that however harsh, however dreadful conditions were there, they were immeasurably better than the hell from which these people had come. I think I have to be very blunt with the Court and say that in the many intervening years since, I've -- I have often speculated whether or not they actually knew who I was. I'm sure they didn't. Whether or not in the mental state they were in, they might have regarded me as being a Serbian plant, whether or not the presence of the television cameras led them to nevertheless even in the absence of their guards tell me things that would not have got them into trouble with their guards, if I had been in their position, suffering the horrors from which they had come, would I have told some unknown person, parachuted into my midst things which could have caused me to lose my life? I'm aware that of all the influences that made me take the decision I took, the influence and the voices of those prisoners running very loud in my head, but was it right? And I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could we look, then, at the rest of the video, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we pause again, please, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, you said as far as you could see, the camp was properly run. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, please bear in mind that I think I was there for more than half an hour. I think it must have been an hour or perhaps even an hour and a half but what I meant by that was there was a fence around the camp, it appeared to be properly in place, it was guarded properly, there were cooking facilities there, it was not total chaos, as I saw in Trnopolje on the following day. Prisoners were lined up and moved about in a professional military manner. There were rudimentary medical facilities, wholly inadequate in my view but nevertheless they existed. It was not chaos it was certainly not perfect, it was certainly not acceptable but it was not disorganised chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you intending by that remark to convey anything about the actual conditions of detention, in other words the food, the accommodation, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I think I made it very clear, I think, in the interview which I gave. I think I used the words that conditions were detestable. They were not what we would have wanted, not what anybody would have wanted but they were at least better from the hell from which they came. The point I was trying to make was that the fact that this was not Golgotha did not make it perfect but at least it made it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we can just finish off the clip, then, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wonder if you would allow me, it came across I think very, very, clearly, the Court may not have been able to pick up the first young man interviewed there but the word he used was "bolje" which is "better" and the second one said "fino" which is "okay," when asked what the conditions were. I think when you make a judgement on this, ten years later, it's very difficult to put this into context but the context in which I think they were expressing and I was expressing was relief and relief that things were better. They were not by any standard acceptable but they were at least better from the complete hell from which they had come and which I expected to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two things out of what was said there. First, it's mentioned that these were civilians. Did you understand that any of the people that you spoke to were actually military persons who had been captured in the course of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I couldn't see any evidence of anything with the single exception I shall come to in a moment which told me that I was looking at soldiers from the front line. And indeed those photographs showed very clearly these looked more to me like farmers. Now that is not to say that in the turmoil of Yugoslavia some of them may not have taken up arms for whatever reason, to defend their property, to exercise revenge but I would be prepared to be very certain that they were not part of an organised or even disorganised military unit. They had neither equipment nor any trace of uniform left, nor did their possessions -- nor did their meagre and pitiful possessions piled around them, well, piled around them, assembled at their -- the place they slept, tell me if anything else that the possessions of ordinary farming or agricultural people. They consisted of a mug, a scrap of photograph of the wife and the family, some clothes they didn't have to -- happen to be at the time wearing in the intense stifling heat so I'm certain that they were not combatants in the accepted sense of the Geneva Convention. The only exception to that was the Canadian mercenary whom I met, who had been shot in the leg and was in a very rudimentary form of plaster in the medical centre and he clearly had been in combat and admitted that he had been part of a regular unit. Indeed, I should point out that the only conversation I had here which did not require interpreters, and I think that's significant, was my conversation with him. Again out of ear shot of the guards but he confirmed he had told me he had not been to Omarska and Keraterm he had come straight into Manjaca but he also confirmed in English and with nobody else present the story that the prisoners had told me about things being better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The interpreter that you took with you, was that somebody who was provided?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that's significant, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well I think again it's a matter with which I subsequently I suppose concerned and worried myself but the truth is that to add to the factors I spoke about earlier on he was an interpreter provided about the Serb authorities so the prisoners would have assumed that anything they would have told me in those private conversations would have been passed back to the Serb authorities, self-evidently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Arising from that, the second matter is this: Did any of the prisoners you spoke to tell you about the deaths of two men, Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't. I would have thought -- I don't know when those deaths took place. I subsequently heard both from people I had met since who were at Manjaca at the time, in various circumstances, that whilst a very significant amount of killing may have gone on substantially before I arrived, around about the time I arrived, and certainly significantly so afterwards when the Red Cross came in. The killings I don't say they ceased but I know of no killing that took place after that event that isn't to say they didn't happen, but I know of none whereas a significant portion appeared to have happened beforehand. I draw the conclusion subsequently which matches the conclusion I made at the time that either around the time I arrived or shortly before, a substantial attempt had been made to, I don't know how shall we put it, regularise, it seems such an inadequate word, attempt to regularise the conditions in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, please, next, to look at some documents that relate to the camp and which I think you saw for the first time yesterday. Could you first of all, please, be shown Exhibit P394? This was a report on the visit by the International Red Cross to the Manjaca prisoner of war camp on the 16th of July, and it begins by stating that "At the urging of the Banja Luka-based International Red Cross from Geneva and in keeping with the agreement signed on the 13th of July, 1992, by Mr. D. Kalanic [phoen] from the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a visit to the prisoner of war camp in Manjaca was granted." Two things. Were you aware first of all of this agreement of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. I was aware of a general agreement, and I don't believe this is the one, but -- made by Karadzic and by Mr. Izetbegovic at the time, that international officials would be provided access to anywhere they sought to go within the two combat areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know, when you got to Manjaca, that the Red Cross had made what appears to be an at least a brief visit to the camp in July?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that. Indeed it features in the letter that I subsequently wrote to Mr. Sommaruga in -- immediately after my visit of the 12th of August in which I said that conditions in the camp were completely unacceptable and I said that I was surprised to learn that the camp was not the subject of regular visits from the ICRC, indeed that there had been a visit which I describe as having been ten days previously, and that's all. Ms. Korner perhaps I could just say at this stage that I had one aim that day, one aim, and that aim was to see what I could do to save the lives of these people and I believed that that was best done by encouraging the Serb authorities who ran the prison, if indeed things had improved over the last days to continue that improvement and to ensure that the Red Cross paid regular visits. They subsequently did and I believe that -- that improvement, slight, and an improvement from horror into unacceptability continued, and I have to say I think the judgement I made, whether in precise detail right or wrong, nevertheless in the sense that it may have contributed to saving lives, was the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd just like you to look at one other part of this document, please, which is on the second page. The report was signed by someone describing himself as the assistant commander for moral guidance, a Colonel Vukelic. Does that name ring any bells with you at all?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'm afraid it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph on that page, they say or he says, "We demanded that in future, they announce their visit at least two to three days in advance, send us a detailed work plan, and do not change the camp's work timetable." Does it surprise you that they, the army, were insisting that there was an announcement two or three days in advance of any visit?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: In what I know now, it certainly doesn't, no. They would have -- I mean, the Serb authorities were now at this stage under the most intense international pressure. It was the number one news story on every international news media, and they realised that what had gone on had been completely unacceptable and what was still going on, though better in Manjaca, was unacceptable so I suspect they would have wanted to give themselves as much time to present the face they would wish to have presented to the world before any Red Cross visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you look, next, please, at a document marked P398? And indeed, 399 at the same time, which are two documents from the same date, the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look first of all at the one that's marked 398, headed, "Reconstruction of the water supply system in the Manjaca military training area, then request," it deals with the fact that the water supply is unsatisfactory. And then it deals with what has to -- should happen, and states, "Please note that there are enough prisoners of war who can be engaged as labourers for the entire length of the water pipes with the appropriate security." The second document, if you can look at that, please, P399, which talks about stepping up security measures and defence of the prisoner of war camp, could you turn to paragraph 3, please, on the second page? It states that there is a combat order, a combat order with a camp defence plan, et cetera, and then states, "On issuing the order conduct an exercise for the units by no later than 1st of August, 1992. During the exercise make sure that the prisoners do not find out about defence variants. Make fox holes and fully fortified VP for troops and combat equipment and camouflage them. Use the prisoners as labourers to make the VP for combat equipment and take every security measure." Lord Ashdown, from your military experience was it acceptable and within the Geneva Conventions to use camp prisoners described as prisoners of war as labourers for water pipes and building whatever VP may be?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner I regret I'm not in any sense an expert on the Geneva Convention but as I recall it, using prisoners for labour, I think in particular to help construct defence mechanisms for war, is illegal under the convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, at --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Sorry, just in case the Court -- it means that I would be more concerned about the second of these two instances than the first. I don't say the first is legal but I'm pretty clear the second is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then, please, could you look at Exhibit P405?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the English version of this document? Could you put that on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this document, dated the 3rd of August, says, again it's an order, from the 1st Krajina Corps command, the local command, "Approval for the visit of the international committee to the detention camps at Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor." It states that on the basis of the verbal order of the Serbian Republic, Bosnia-Herzegovina, army main Staff Commander, a visit by the international committee and a team of reporters to the detention camps in Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor within the next two days is approved. In this regard, all measures are to be taken to make the condition -- to make conditions in these camps satisfactory. This implies order, cleanliness, functional medical care, accurate record and so on and so forth. Wherever representatives of the detainees have contact with the camp authorities have not been selected this is to be done urgently. Camp wardens must prepare for briefings and escort of the committee and reporters. This assignment is urgent and any barring of visits to the camp is out of the question." I don't imagine that you were aware that an order had been sent out to clean up these camps in advance of the visits but does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That coincides exactly with the impression that I got at the time and which is recorded in my diary, that a -- an improvement even to totally unacceptable standards but from appalling ones had recently been undertaken and was under way and it was my concern to ensure that that improvement continued as that was the only way to save the lives of those who were there. So I am completely unsurprised. Indeed, I have to say somewhat reassured, that this provides evidence for what I -- for my judgement at the time. Can I just add one thing? I am able to give the Court a judgement based on necessarily rather skimpy evidence of a, as I recall it, an hour's visit, of how things were when I got there. It would be completely inappropriate in my view, indeed it would be extremely dangerous for anybody to assume that the conditions I found were the conditions which that camp had been operating on before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then could you look now, please, briefly at the last two documents, first Exhibit P408? A document dated three days later, 6th of August, selection of prisoners in the Manjaca prisoner of war camp, and it states that, "By processing the war prisoners in the Manjaca POW camp, we realise that a certain [quite large number of them, according to incrimination] do not deserve to be treated as prisoners of war. They did not have weapons. They did not participate in combat. They were not in uniform." And then it deals with there should be a selection of people who can be released. According to our records, in the Manjaca POW camp, there are currently 944 prisoners from the Sanski Most municipality. As you know we have recently been attacked by the European and world media in connection with the existence of concentration camps so this is sufficient reason to carry out a prisoner selection." Now you had these conversations and we saw you on video with Colonel Popovic. Did he tell you that it had been decided that a number of these people shouldn't have been there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. He did tell me that he had recently received I think he said 1.400 people from Omarska and Keraterm and these would of course be added to the 944 mentioned here but he did not tell me that these were not prisoners of war. In fact he, as I recall it, consistently claimed that they were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recall mention by anybody and you may not, of the Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I remember Sanski Most being one of those names which among so many myriad others were in the press as scenes of horror but beyond that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. And then finally, please, could you look at Exhibit -- Your Honour this is not yet been made an exhibit. It's the document dated the 7th of August, with the disclosure number 4.55 on it. And it will be Exhibit P1534 -- 1535, sorry. Do Your Honours have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- there are only two items. This was a more general report. If we look under paragraph 3 in the translation, "Situation in the area," it talks about fighting and then it says this: "About 1.460 POWs were brought from Omarska to the Manjaca POW camp. There were deaths during transport to the camp." Did Colonel Popovic mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner, he didn't. The 1.400 or so he did mention. The deaths, he didn't. What is Manjaca from Omarska and Prijedor? I don't know, 40 kilometres, 30 kilometres, something like that. It's -- yes, well, I think the Court can draw its own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if you look over the page under paragraph 5, please, it is said there that the issue of the POW camp at Manjaca is becoming complex in terms of physical security and especially in regard to supplies, cooking, water and health protection. And so on. I think you told us you yourself saw the basic amenities that were available to the prisoners at the camp?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, basic would be the right word. Rudimentary, totally inadequate might be another. I did see food being ladled out. It was -- it was food. I think the thing that worried me more than anything else was the appalling physical condition of these people, malnutrition and wounds and sores and the bit that worried me the most was this was August, winter was coming, this is a bitterly, bitterly cold part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and lying as they were completely without covering on the bare earth of these -- I thought they were tank maintenance sheds but looking at the pictures it's clear they are in fact cattle sheds, many people would lose their lives not necessarily through deliberate action but just through neglect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I want to move now, please, to the following day, when you paid a visit to Trnopolje. That was on the 11th of August. If we look at your diary entry, you went there, I think, with a military escort; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: A police escort. The genesis of this visit was that when we got back from Manjaca, the previous night, I was approached by Penny Marshall of ITN who told me of the existence of what she described as a civilian detention camp. I was any way wishing the following day to go down to Prijedor, passing through the Kozarac area, where I hoped to be able to pay a visit to Omarska and Keraterm but by now these camps were either being substantially emptied or had been emptied as I understood, and I agreed with Ms. Marshall that having visited the authorities in Prijedor, I should then return and join her in Trnopolje because she believed, and I concluded that she was correct, that at this stage, Trnopolje was an area where press attention would save lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that -- I'm sorry, you stated in your diary that as you drove towards Trnopolje, this is the bottom of the page Tuesday, the 11th, you passed village after village which had been burnt out completely, and you recorded clearly one of the worst areas for ethnic cleansing, this, it looked dreadful and "quite shock me." You told us how you had driven through areas on your way up to Banja Luka which had been ethnically cleansed, as it were. How did these roads around Prijedor compare to what you had earlier seen?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, they were worse, if it's possible to be worse, than what Brcko looked like at the time in the war but they were worse in this sense, that in the other villages I had seen, by and large, individual houses, individual groups of houses, would have been torched and destroyed and it's important to say, Ms. Korner, that this happened on all sides. It wasn't just Serbs doing this to Muslims, it was all three ethnicities doing to each other. What I think, however, made this area the Kozarac area stand out was that here whole villages, without exception, had been torched and destroyed. It was a land completely laid waste.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think you in fact then went to the Prijedor police and administrative headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you describe there meeting someone who you thought was the local army commander, "A huge bull of a man, with a very powerful frame, but I thought rather kindly eyes, and then someone who had described himself as the mayor and if there was a villain, I suspect that was it, narrow and cold eyes." You added a comment. I want you to have a look, please, at a photograph of two men. I appreciate it's a long time ago, and just see whether either of these men are recognisable to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this is not on the list but it's one of the ones that have already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While it's being looked for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit P1128-24 and we'll have it put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do either of those two men look familiar?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: They do. It is ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think I would be -- I think as my memory recalls it, they are certainly two that I have seen before, I could only have seen them I suspect at this time. As I recall it, Ms. Korner, the gentleman in the military uniform was one of those with whom I had the contention in Banja Luka the night before going to Manjaca. Indeed I think he was almost certainly the most senior one there, the one who was stopping us going to Manjaca but I may be wrong about that. The one on the right is the -- is one of the ones I saw at Prijedor, yes, I'm pretty sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. You can take that away again. Now, Trnopolje itself. You gave a description in your diary of what you found. You said that it was an indescribable sight of squalor. There were no facilities. The Red Cross were there when you arrived. And then the ITN crew as well. Then you describe that there were a few wounded lying on filthy fly-blown mattresses and you described them in the playing field were camped a miserable heap of humanity people who had come with almost nothing and in some case literally nothing. You -- some were lying out in the sun, others under makeshift awnings, suitable for shade but hopeless when it rained. You stopped and talked to some of them and some -- in one area, there was a rough earth lavatory with a few blocks around it to give some brief privacy. Four of these for 3.000 people. And you then described the conversation that you had with people. Now, that's how you described in the diary. Looking back now, do you still retain an image of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly do. I think it was -- listen, there were terrible things and terrible sights in the Balkans but I can never remember one that I saw in my experience - my experience is limited one needs to remember - worse than this, and I can recall the sight to my eye very easily. It was, Ms. Korner in my view, worse than Manjaca. It was worse for a number of reasons, precisely because there was no order. However brutal and inappropriate the order of Manjaca might have been it was nevertheless order. Here was chaos but it was worse for another reason. At least in Manjaca what I saw were men relatively young men. Here were the old, the infirm, the wounded, women, children, simply herded together on this school playing field, hopeless, futureless, despairing, most had completely lost any dignity. The toilet facilities were such that men and women had to use them. They were completely inadequate. People were defecating on the ground. All the personal privacy which gives people dignity had been robbed from them. At night, as I was told, I can't verify this myself, they were subject to the depredations of Serb extremists who came in, took the women, took them away, as was described to me. I can't verify this. Raped them and either killed them or returned them to the camp the following day, to such an extent that the local Serb population of Trnopolje took pity on the people camped in their midst and sought to protect them from the depredations of these extremists which I found both moving and astonishing. It was an unbearable scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that the local Serbs took pity on them. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was told that by some of the -- by some of those, you can't call them inmates, by some of this what I -- squalid miserable heap of humanity. Those to whom I spoke said to me, as I recall, one of our problems is we don't have a wire fence around us. There is nothing to protect us from the outside. And so at night, the wolves come in and they said the local Serbs who live there are decent people and have sought to protect us from this but what can they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recall now whether you spoke to anybody who appeared to be in charge of this camp?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. I could find no one in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any sign of any guards at all?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. I can -- there were military in the area. There were police in the area. Police I think more than military. There was a docile population to the extent to which as we drove there, little knots of women and old men and children were walking the lanes that led to it under the boiling sun, clearly being ordered to go there and docilely obeying that order. I think -- I recall them saying that they were told this was a transit camp from which they would be moved on or moved back or handed over to the Muslim authorities, and of course, as we subsequently know, a matter of a couple or three days or short number of days after I was there, some of them were indeed taken away, up on to the Vlasic and tipped off the cliffs to their deaths.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to deal finally with the letters that Lord Ashdown wrote and one press release but it may be this is the appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We should be having the break in about six minutes time, so if you prefer to stop now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it would be probably simpler to deal with the documents as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we will do that. So we'll have a short coffee break and we'll resume in 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, I'm going to come in a moment to the letters that you wrote after your visit but I'd like you please to have a look at a transcript that was made of an interview that you apparently gave to Banja Luka Television.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours this was marked 7.230. I think you've got a copy and if the witness could be handed the copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1537. Because I'm going to exhibit the letters as 1536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, this is apparently a statement made by you to Banja Luka Television on the 11th of August after your visit. And you made a statement as follows, according to them, or this document, "First of all I have to say that I've been a soldier myself and know that what I have seen are no concentration camps." What did you have in mind when you -- if this is an accurate record of what you said obviously?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did give an interview that night to Banja Luka TV, and this appears to me to be an accurate excerpt, may I underline the word excerpt of that in the nature of all television interviews, they tend to be cut and this by my recollection of the interview which was a long one, certainly has been cut, and when I used the word "concentration camp" I was of course thinking of what the accepted term for a concentration camp is which is Belsen, Auschwitz-Birkenau, and indeed, if I may Ms. Korner because it may turn on to the questions you may ask me in relation to my subsequent letters, I refer again to that definition in the letter which I subsequently wrote to Mr. Karadzic which I can explain more in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then the condition -- you went on apparently to say, "The conditions for life in this camp are hard but with regards to the situation all should try to better the conditions. A lot ought to be done but it is most important that in these detention centres, the Geneva Conventions are complied with."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Again, you need to put this in the context, as I recall very clearly the previous bits of this interview which have -- appear to have been cut, I described those conditions in considerably more detail and said that they were unacceptable but in this excerpt, the context in which I'm trying to make an essentially a political comment was that these camps appeared to have been subject to a programme of regularisation which was improving them and I wanted that to continue. It would have been unhelpful to that attempt to describe things other than in rather objective -- in these objective terms. The important point about the next sentence is of course that it's important that in these detention camps, the Geneva Conventions are complied with rather than a statement that they have been complied with. This is an attempt to get the Serb authorities to apply the Geneva Convention in the future even if they haven't in the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then you go on to say that "The International Red Cross should be included in the work of the centre and that you personally have tried to make them come as often as possible. The second thing to be done is to provide help but in this case, the conditions for the prisoners would be better than for the people outside the prison." What did you mean by that, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It would be better for the people, rather than -- the word "than" is I'm sure an intrusion into perhaps the translation here. It would be better for people if they were outside the prison rather than inside. Again, I had two -- I had three aims which I was trying to achieve here. One was to ensure that any improvement that had taken place in the last two to three days would continue. Secondly, to get the Red Cross in. That was I suppose my primary aim on a regular basis. I have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. informed by prisoners I've met since that shortly after my arrival, the Red Cross did indeed come in on regular visits and from the next visit, I have been informed by prisoners I've met that they were numbered and after that, conditions substantially improved. And the third was building on a statement, a conversation that I'd had with Dr. Karadzic which you will see reflected in the letter, was to ensure that the exchange of prisoners should take place as soon as possible so that these people were -- got out of these camps and into a safer environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you went on to state, "I also appeal to foreign media to put pressure to show the conditions of Serbs on the other side are subjected to." At that stage, did you consider it important that there should be reporting of what was happening in other areas?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, look, the truth is that there were no clean hands in this war, that atrocities took place on all sides. I've no doubt that the mistreatment of prisoners almost certainly took place on all sides. If I am to make a subjective judgement, I believe that the weight of atrocities was very heavily on the Serb side rather than on any other but I don't pretend for a second that there were not black deeds done by all, and my concern was to -- I reasoned as follows: That if all sides could be subjected to pressure to treat prisoners properly, then the conditions of all prisoners would improve, if there was evidence of an even-handed approach from the press, then the Serb authorities would be -- find it easier to respond, and if there was evidence of appropriate treatment on Croat and Muslim sides, then that would produce an improvement of treatment of their prisoners in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think that's all that I want to ask you about that because I think the rest of it was dealing with effectively the same type of thing. So can we come now, please, then to the letters that you wrote to a number of people, at the end of your visit there? If we can start, please, with the one that was numbered attachment to your letter to Mr. Major, Prime Minister Major who was then in power?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour can I ask that all these letters be exhibited under one exhibit number which is P1536? And this will be P1536.1? It's dated the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you set out the background to your visit, and then your views on the western powers having acted or not. Could you come to the second page? You dealt with, in a paragraph, "Let me describe to you why this matter is so urgent." And you describe the conditions at Trnopolje, effectively very much I think as you described them in your diary?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in fact, you didn't mention in this particular letter Manjaca. I think we will see that you mentioned it in other letters but not in this one?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The purpose of this letter which I composed on my way back driving from Trnopolje to Belgrade that night was to do two things, was to try and convince the British government and through them western governments that their policy of inactivity in this war was wrong and indeed dangerous, and secondly, to draw particular attention to the conditions of Trnopolje. Please remember that this was the event which I -- is seared on my memory still which was most fresh in my mind when I wrote this letter and when I constructed these letters it seemed to me best to bring these conditions to light in the letters to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Sommaruga of the International Red Cross. I concentrated on the Manjaca camp because they seemed to be the most appropriate authorities to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move then to your letter to Dr. Karadzic which was attachment 3 and will become whatever it is 1536.2? And as you say there, you thanked him for making the trip possible. In the second paragraph saying that you wished to look at the effect of the war and see what could be done in the short term to halt or reduce the intensity and to relieve the suffering of innocent people caught in the middle. And then you went on to deal with Manjaca and you told him you were attaching the copy of the letter that you wrote to Mr. Sommaruga and stated in the third paragraph, "I was also pleased to see that the camp commandant appeared to be observing the conditions of the Geneva Convention as far as his resources would allow." I think you've probably explained that but by that sentence what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Precisely that at the time I was there, an attempt to apply the Geneva Conventions seemed to be in progress. That is not to say that that was the case before I got there, that one of the factors was a limitation of resources and that indeed is reflected in some of the previous evidence that you have shown. But as I continue, food remains at a very low level, especially for those recovering from such a long period of malnutrition, living conditions are sparse and medical provisions rudimentary and inadequate for people who are still very weak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Sorry Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The impression I'm seeking to convey there is that though the conditions have improved they remain unacceptable and that improvement has to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because if you look at the second page you say exactly that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "I believe that from what I was able to see, it would be both irresponsible and inaccurate to call those camps which I visited concentration camps within the meaning that has come to be accepted for that term."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: And here of course, I refer -- that last phrase is intended to mean what is it that we know of concentration camps that they are in the modern parlance have become accepted to mean extermination camps of the kind that Belsen and Auschwitz were and in my view Keraterm and Omarska were and this did not fit that category. Ms. Korner, it's probably important for the Court to realise that it would have been no service to the political aim, i.e., the saving of lives, if I had used stronger terms than the phrase "within the meaning that has come to be accepted for that term." But it's clearly indicating to Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic that although this wasn't Belsen, that did not make it acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say in the next sentence, "Nevertheless, conditions remain unacceptable and have to be improved with urgency." You then dealt with the arrivals from Omarska and the prisoner exchange and then in the penultimate paragraph on that it page stated: "Let me add that as I was deeply concerned that as we were driving about we saw Muslim villages totally destroyed. It is insufficient to say that the same is being done on the other side. It is wrong. It is barbaric and ought to be stopped by the leaders of both sides." If we can move then to the --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: May I just stop you, one of the most important points for me to make to Dr. Karadzic in this letter was the point made in the second paragraph of that letter which raises the point of which I had by this stage become convinced, that those who I saw were not combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. As you say you make that point very strongly. The third letter of that date or the one we have driven as the third, attachment 4 was written to General Nambiar. Was he in charge of UNPROFOR at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: He was, based in Zagreb and this talks about the very specific position of Gorazde at that stage, subject to a siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't think that we need trouble with that. And then finally, so that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes and then the final letter to Mr. Sommaruga, the President of the International Red Cross, and in the second paragraph, you say, "In the course of your -- the tour you referred to, "We had the chance to visit the prisoner of war camp at Manjaca, and in inverted commas refugee camp at Trnopolje." What made you use that expression, refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's how it was described to me at the time. I suppose a more accurate expression might have been internment camp but they were all refugees so I called it a refugee camp, displaced persons camp might be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you go on to deal with the -- what you were told by Colonel Popovic, that the camp had not been visited by the ICRC for more than ten days and went on to express your concerns and then if we go to the next page, the third paragraph, "The Serbian authorities tell me that food shortages in the country and the effects of the international sanctions are limiting the resources that they have at their disposal. I am unable to judge the veracity of this and it must be said that every prisoner to whom I spoke [out of ear shot of the guards] informed me that conditions here are much better than those in the camps from which they came. But I regret that this tells us more about the unacceptability of the camps from which they came than it does about the acceptability of Manjaca. I accept that the Serb authorities are making a serious attempt to put matters right on an urgent basis but that does not mean that matters can rest here." You mentioned that you'd spoken to the Canadian mercenary but other than that, were most of the people that you spoke to in Manjaca those who had come from Omarska or Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think the vast majority. We were there for a limited period of time, although I was -- they sought to persuade me to go and see other prisoners I decided that those from Omarska and Keraterm were at most threat to their lives and I spent by far and away most time there. In fact, my memory may be failing me but I don't recall speaking, apart from those I found in the medical centre, a matter of four or five, of whom one was the Canadian mercenary, apart from those, I don't recollect speaking to anybody other than those who came from Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. That will then be .4, Your Honour. Finally this, Lord Ashdown, you paid a number of visits to the territories of the former Yugoslavia and you've testified in other cases about that. How would you sum up your visit to those camps in comparison to the other matters, the other times you visited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to object to that unless we are a little more specific about what camps and when, what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- I'm asking about the visit to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help by simply saying that I don't believe in all my life I've done a better day's work than I did at Manjaca. It's not often given to us that we have a chance to participate in the saving of lives, but I believe, and conversations I've had with Manjaca prisoners subsequently lead me to believe that on that day, because of the improvement of conditions, the consequence was that lives were saved. In respect of Trnopolje, I have to say that I feel haunted by the thought that if somehow or another we could have done more, the lives of those people who were slaughtered by being thrown over the cliffs a matter of a few days later may have been prevented so I suppose I'd say that the 11th -- the 10th of August I regard as the best days work I've ever done, the 11th of August I regard as being one of the most questionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that answer your objection, Mr. Ackerman? Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lord Ashdown, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I take it, Ms. Korner, that you're not going to tender as exhibits what was attachment 8 and attachment 9?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct. Sorry, attachment 9 is the diary I've already exhibited that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's but attachment 8 you haven't tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Is that the press reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not bothering to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman will be cross-examining you now. Mr. Ackerman please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, good morning. My name is John Ackerman. I represent Mr. Brdjanin. I come from the United States and I must say this you're the first lord to whom I've ever spoken for any reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I would forget the title. I don't regard it as important any more other than a description of the place I work and my job description. I never use it and I would be grateful if it was used as little as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'll call you sir or -- but something to -- there is some deference due to you for your position, I'm sure of that. I'm going to try to -- I know that you are a busy man and that you want to leave here as soon as you possibly can and I'm going to try my best to move through this material as rapidly as I can, consistent with what the interpreters need from us, and consistent with you having a -- as full an opportunity to answer my questions as you feel that you need. That would be fair, I think, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It would indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to begin my questions of you with a statement that you gave, of fairly recent vintage, to an investigator from the Prosecution by the name of Richard Dupas on 9 May, 2002. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I do recall giving a variety of statements. I don't think I can recall the one on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like a copy of it just so you can?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It might be useful, Mr. Ackerman, I don't know. If it's immediately available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please. Document with ERN number 02193824. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, part of what I wanted to ask you about that I think has now been cleared up and that is when you spoke to Banja Luka Television and when you talked about that in your statement to Mr. Dupas here, what you were talking about when you were speaking to Banja Luka Television was what you had observed after you had been to Manjaca and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. After I'd been to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'd not been to Trnopolje. That was the night I came back from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and witness please break between question and answer?
