utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have to break between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One of the microphones is not switched on. And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I say that again? No, the statement was given on the night that I returned from Manjaca, the night before I went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the impressions that you gained then, regarding Manjaca, was based basically on a couple of things, your own personal observations, what you saw and heard while were you there, plus conversations that you had with some of the inmates out of the ear shot of the camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the second is part of the first but that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in these conversations, out of the ear shot of camp authorities, I take it you did not learn of any deaths from beatings or otherwise that had occurred at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, the answer to your question is no, I did not learn of them. It would have been surprising if indeed if I had given that my conversation within what the press describe as half an hour I recall as an hour's visit were necessarily brief and confined to their personal conditions rather than the history or what had occurred in recent days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it the case that some of the men you talked to preferred staying in Manjaca to being released out of fear that they would be pressured to fight for their own ethnic army?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman. It's certainly not the case. They certainly expressed the view that if released, they may have been required to go and fight, but though I didn't ask them the specific question to which you refer, I am absolutely confident that if I had said to those people, "You can walk out the gates and fend for yourself," they would have gone immediately and with great relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look, sir, at the last sentence of your statement that I've just given you, where I got that idea was what you're reputed to have said there, "Some of the men I spoke to were afraid that if they left, pressure would be put on them to fight for their own ethnic army."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Of course. But that does not, I think, infer a preference to be in the camp rather than out. That was a fear that they had if they should leave. But I put it to you that all the evidence that I received was that the fear that they would have had from remaining there would have been greater. They were merely saying to me that leaving here, though infinitely preferable than being here does not make me without risk in this war. A perfectly ordinary belief, I'm sure you would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wouldn't you think that some of them might have felt and might even in the way they expressed to you, that as bad as Manjaca was, it was safer than a trench in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Mr. Ackerman. I have to say to you that I am completely confident, if you had given these people the opportunity to leave the hands of the Serbs in the light of their experiences in Omarska and Keraterm and their experiences in Manjaca, they would have gone anywhere on earth and put themselves in anybody else's hands except those in whose hands they currently were. Of that I am completely confident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also said this, and you've talked about it this morning, and to some extent you've answered the question, you said, "There were very few combatants that I saw but the majority appeared to be civilians." And I think the way you described that in your testimony this morning was they just looked like ordinary farmers to you.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well if you recall, Mr. Ackerman, I said to you that it wasn't just what they looked like. I have met many soldiers who looked like ordinary farmers but it was the complete absence of uniforms, the complete absence of for instance footwear of the sort that you need to be a combat soldier, the complete absence of equipment, the complete absence of anything relating to military equipment and above all, the presence of the pathetic possessions of farmers plucked out of the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the conclusion you made there was based on the lack of the accoutrements that one would ordinarily see from a military man?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Accoutrements, bearing, I've been experienced enough in the military to be able to know a soldier when I see one, whether in uniform or out. They were not in a physical condition which showed they'd been subject to any kind of military training. Their bearing was one of an absence of military discipline, their position was absolutely consistent with -- I want to say innocent -- I can't pretend that all of them would have been innocent but ordinary people plucked out of ordinary lives and put into this hell hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're speaking, sir, of the kind of military organisation that you were part of or -- and that I was part of in the United States where we in fact have significant training and all of that. Aren't you aware that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to some extent even the Serb army, was made up of people who were actually literally plucked from the fields, thrown into a uniform given a gun and told go and fight?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I certainly recognise that description, what I saw of the Bosnian army, it does not apply to what I saw of most of the Serb army but yes, it is perfectly possible. I can only give you the judgement that I made at the time, which was that the majority of people I had seen were those who had been burnt and brutalised out of the houses that I had seen on the way to Manjaca, and that as such, their condition, their language, their bearing, their equipment, was entirely consistent with the fact that a matter of days or weeks before, they had been the inhabitants of those houses I had seen destroyed in such great numbers along the road to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bear with me a moment while I find what I'm looking for. Here we go. Do you still have your diaries in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, and there is a page number at the top, big long number, 02195557, it has a number 14 circled on it. I don't know if yours does or not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're talking about being at Manjaca. The second paragraph from the top, "I went off to have a look at the medical facilities which are pathetic but then there are a few medical supplies getting through anywhere because of the embargo on medicines." What was the embargo on medicines that you spoke about there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well, there was a point consistently made to me by Karadzic and others, and of course, you'll understand the political importance of this point when I repeat it to you, that one of the reasons you might arguably say one of the excuses, why they were unable to provide full medical facilities, was because of the west's sanctions which also meant sanctions on the provision of medical equipment. I think I recalled discovering later on that the west's sanctions at this stage did not apply to medical equipment but that is the argument that was consistently being made to me so you find it reflected in my diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you -- you of course didn't during your visit have an opportunity to go to the hospital in Banja Luka and compare the medical supplies available there with those that you saw in other places, did you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but on the other hand on a subsequent visit, I did go -- Your Honour I'm afraid I can't lay my hands on this but I could certainly do so if I'm given access to my diaries, I did go to the veterans prison in Pale which was the Serb headquarters close to Sarajevo and saw medical facilities there, and although I wouldn't claim that they matched those in modern western hospitals, they were of a substantially -- substantially better sort than I saw in Manjaca operating equipment, nurses, doctors, the provision of medical facilities. So although on this occasion, I didn't look at Banja Luka, within, I think, five or six months of this, if I recall during my visit in December I was able to see Serb military hospitals, Serb civilian hospitals in Pale and I can tell you there was no comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you didn't see that same facility at the same time in August, did you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Self-evidently not but I have absolutely no reason to believe that what I would have seen in Banja Luka at the beginning of the war, when supplies were more plenty full would have been worse than what I saw in Pale several months later when medical supplies were later in the war much less available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you -- were you aware that the Banja Luka region, that Krajina region, basically became an island that was cut off from its normal source of supplies of all kinds?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me finish my question. The border with Croatia was closed, the Croats closed -- the Croats and Muslim forces closed that corridor that connected the Krajina and Serbia, that was another source of supplies. The opportunities for air supply were limited because of the no-fly issues. So that getting supplies into that area was very, very, very difficult at that period of time, including food and medicine?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: There were UN supplies coming in and certainly, the offer of UN supplies, in much the same way as to Sarajevo but the answer to your question is, yes, I was. It was difficult enough for us to get from Pale through the Posavina corridor which was subject to ambushes from all sides, very narrow corridor, and I'm sure conditions were not easy for that element of the Republika Srpska as we now know it though I venture to say that Banja Luka being the capital town, being in an area of far larger geographical population density than the other portion of Republika Srpska around Pale was nevertheless in a far better condition than Sarajevo, which at that stage was subject to a siege. I could accept, and I will accept, that medical supplies and other facilities were not as you would see them in a western country. I could not accept, however, that this early in the war, the conditions you described had only been in place for a month or so, there were insufficient medical supplies to be able to provide better facilities for Manjaca in what was the largest remaining territory of Serb occupation -- occupied areas and within two miles of its capital city.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The UN supplies that you say were coming in, I'm operating totally off the top of my head here, sir, so you may correct me --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think we both are, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... UN supplies were coming in at that stage I recall most of them however being refused by the Serb authorities under those circumstances. They built up to greater intensity later when the conditions of Serbs within the Serb-occupied areas were considerably depleted by the length of the war. But this, let me remind you, was within two months of the start of the war and five miles of the capital city.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My memory is that UN convoys trying to come into that area from Croatia, from Zagreb, were only being allowed in if they were giving as much as 80 per cent of that to the Croats as sort of a fee for getting across the border. Do you recall anything about that at all?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I think we are both on area which we are not terribly certain about here. I certainly am. Let me say that before I came in here in July, I went through Croatia and the war had by and large stopped then. All the supplies moving in to Bosnia were coming through Zagreb and I remember seeing them, in fact I flew in with a collection of supplies going into Sarajevo in July, and I do not recall anybody saying to me that the Croats were taking a cut on the way through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to the time that you went to Manjaca and Trnopolje, you were aware of journalistic activity and that camps in that area had been portrayed like World War II vintage concentration camps by some media, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: They were portrayed and by all the evidence I knew and now know they were like World War II extermination camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told Karadzic in your letter to him regarding at least what you saw at Manjaca and Trnopolje and Ms. Korner asked you about this, "It would be irresponsible and inaccurate to call those camps which I visited concentration camps within the meaning that has come to be accepted for that term." And I fully accept everything you've already said about that. I don't see any necessity for you to repeat it unless you want to comment a little further regarding my question?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think I've explained what I was seeking to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it there is no reason for us to believe that you were not able to see at Manjaca and Trnopolje, the same things that the journalists were able to see?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ackerman, I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer that question, Lord Ashdown, I think you have to put it in a time frame, Mr. Ackerman. We need to know for sure that the journalists you were talking about saw what they saw and what you're asking Lord Ashdown about, on the same day or approximately the same date. Because otherwise, there could be a great difference even on the basis of what Lord Ashdown said earlier on this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was imprecise and I'll make it more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you went to Manjaca and Trnopolje, you went in both places there were journalists with you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question is just this: You have no reason to believe that the journalists were able to see anything that you weren't able to see, do you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No. Those journalists who were with me saw what I was able to see. I'm just -- I have a recollection, and it does appear in the video, that at some stage, probably before I left but maybe only five minutes, ten minutes before I left, the journalists were hustled out. You did in fact see that on the video. It may be that I saw more than they did but I have no reason to believe that they saw more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm looking at your diary now from the 8th of August and that would be a three circled. Do you have those numbers circled on yours?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it would be page 3, I guess?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at this point you're at the Intercontinental Hotel in Belgrade and about halfway down through that paragraph, that middle paragraph there, you say this: "CNN has been publishing words about concentration camps and all the press are pretty frightened by this since that is exactly what they are not, and the press believe that this will make the trip even more dangerous."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: You will see, Mr. Ackerman, that there is a manuscript amendment to that. It may not be very clear on yours but I should remind you that these manuscript amendments were made within days of the diary being dictated, which is -- it says that is exactly what the Serbs say they are not. There is a small manuscript amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I see that now, yes?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: There was very considerable nervousness, the press were saying these were concentration camps, the Serbs were extremely angry about this description on so they believed, the press believed, that this would make the trip even more dangerous. Perhaps if would help the Court if I were to say that diaries are inevitably done late at night, pretty tired, and so the words you choose aren't either necessarily molten prose or indeed precisely the words you would have chosen. That's why in this case, as in a very small number of others in my diary I called for the diaries to be returned to me as soon as they were typed and I made the manuscript amendments which then formed part of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those words were chosen on the day of the events and your words today are ten years after the events?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, by no means, those words are included in the manuscript version --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: A matter of days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about your testimony today is ten years after the event?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It is indeed ten years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whereas your diaries were made almost contemporaneously with the event?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As long as we are on that page, you had an occasion there to meet a journalist who you've told us today was actually Ed Vulliamy and who you now know wrote a book about his experiences there, correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your diary what you said about him was, "He strikes me as being thoroughly cut up by the whole affair. That's not going to make life easier. We need people who can make rational judgements in this situation." That implies that you arrived at a conclusion that Vulliamy was not able to make rational judgements. True?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it may imply that. I don't think it means anything as heavy as that but let me say this to you. Mr. Vulliamy is somebody I met late at night and for the first time on this occasion. He was extremely emotionally disturbed by what he was seeing, what rational human being would not be? I made a judgement of him that night, which implies, as you correctly say, that somehow or other, his objectivity might have been affected by this. It was an admonition to myself as much as anything else, that whatever I saw ought not to disturb my objectivity but I'm bound to say that from everything I've known of Mr. Vulliamy since, and we have become I won't say friends but frequent discussers of events in the Balkans, there is nothing that leads me to believe that he is not a journalist of the very highest calibre whose objectivity has not and would not have been disturbed by any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to page 8 of your diary, and this is Sunday, the 9th of August, when you're in Pale and you're taken to Kula, which you described as a show camp?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think this -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And down near the bottom, you talk about having a chat with one or two of the prisoners and then you say this: "A German reporter from Der Spiegel said that she had privately been told by the prisoners that they had been kept inside for four months, that they had not slept where we were shown they had slept and they had not had any food." Then you commented about that: "If this is true, then they didn't look like it. There was no sign that these -- of these people had not been out in the sun a good deal nor any sign that they had not been reasonably well fed."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: For sometime. I add at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, for sometime. I think what you were saying there, and you correct me if I'm wrong, and I know you will, that whatever these people had told this German reporter, if they had told her the things that she told you they told her, did not appear to you to be correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then, if you over a couple of pages to page 10 --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman it would be worthwhile not just going over a couple of pages without drawing attention to the fact to the first paragraph on page 9. This is clearly a show camp. That's what I was brought there for. I was brought there for a propaganda exercise to a show camp and I think it's important just to underline that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I said that when we started, what you called a show camp. Go please, now, to page 10. You talk about having a meal with Karadzic around 1.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You found him refreshingly honest, saying that of course, Serbs had committed atrocities, as others had, but these were all Serbs who were out of control. He could not control every single Serb in the whole area. That's what he told you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your letter to him, which --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Ackerman, I have no wish to add things you would not wish me to touch on but that was the claim. I must say what I saw about the Serb military forces who were in control of the area through which I passed led me to a totally different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we are going to come to that pretty soon, we will talk about that in greater length in a little while. On the 12th of August, you wrote a letter to Mr. Karadzic. On the second page of that letter, I assume you have it there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph down, and you were talking about the prisoners you'd seen from Manjaca: "I believe that the very best thing that can happen to these prisoners is that they are exchanged as soon as possible." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any impediments to that happening, to those people being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes. The mechanisms for exchange had not at this early stage of the war been set up. And each side was blaming the other for not setting it up, not an uncommon practice in the Balkans incidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to your -- let's see if I can -- I'm going to go back to your diary again we are going to go to the 11th of August, please. And it would be page 16. You are talking about the trip you were taking from Banja Luka to Trnopolje where you were escorted by police and you say that you were escorted up to a point where there was a crossroads, they stopped there, said they couldn't take you any further, because they didn't know where Trnopolje was. And that you'd have to wait until some police came who did know where Trnopolje was to escort you further. Essentially that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It's what they said, Mr. Ackerman, yes. I have to tell you that knowing the Balkans a little better than I did on my second visit, I think it is simply inconceivable they didn't know where Trnopolje was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You made another comment there and this comment must have been based on something more than just that event. You said, "I am constantly amazed," which means you've been amazed more than once I assume, "I am constantly amazed at how little people travel here and how much they do not know of their next door area even quite senior people." Right?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's certainly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was something you apparently had found to be kind of universally characteristic of the people you had met in Bosnia up to that point?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: If I thought it was universally characteristic I was universally wrong. Please remember that this is my second trip to the Balkans it is a very, very complex area indeed. Not all the judgements you make about any country are going to be accurate and that one was an inaccurate judgement. Let me say this: That it is true that one of the features of the Balkans I find amazing is that ordinary people travel very little. They probably haven't been up the mountain that so excites a westerner to climb which has been neighbouring their village all their lives. They probably many of them won't have been to their capital but the idea that those who run these countries do not know them or travel extensively across them and that applies to the police as I think -- if I gained that impression it was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the comments that you made in your diary about Trnopolje, and I'm now on page 17, in a paragraph that begins with the language, "In the sleeping areas themselves," you say, "In fact such as the pitiable nature of their condition," you probably meant such is, "that some Serbs had actually protected the area themselves from the depravations of the Serb extremists who came at night robbing, beating and raping the women," so you were told, and then you add, "But there was a terrible breeder of exaggerations." In other words you left room there for some of those stories being exaggerations, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I take you back Mr. Ackerman to that conversation with Mr. Vulliamy. I'm trying here to be as objective as I can. The one thing I very soon discovered is that not all things that you are told by any given nationality in the Balkans is an exact representation of the facts and I know from personal experience that the horror and terror of war does breed exaggeration so of course, I'm leaving myself room for doubt here and I am doing what I suppose in the Court would be saying this is hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will also come to that issue in a little more detail later too. I want to talk now about your letter to John Major. At the time, John Major of course was the Prime Minister, correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were the leader of the Liberal Party?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The Liberal Democrats, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Had you run against him in the immediately preceding election?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The date is 1992. Had I run against him? Not in his own seat but yes I'd been the leader of one party and he was the leader of another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in other words if the voting had gone the right way, you would have been Prime Minister instead of him?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think the voting would have had to have gone a long way the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're right but it was possible?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I don't think there are many political commentators in Britain who would have thought it was possible, Mr. Ackerman but it's fair to say that I tried to pretend it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke of your visit to Trnopolje when you wrote to him, and I think it would be fair to say that you were his political opponent?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was a member of the opposition party, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What they call the loyal opposition?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, the word "loyal" may or may not be attached to the way I behaved but that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to come to that too. There is a lot coming here. What I want to know is when you addressed him about Trnopolje, what you were trying to do is persuade him to take some action?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That you thought needed to be taken?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: Did you in any way exaggerate your report to him regarding Trnopolje for that reason, to make it sound worse than what you'd really seen in an effort to goad him into action?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The answer is, Mr. Ackerman, I must let history be the Judge of that, compare the letter with my diary I think you'll find they match in tone and fact. I made it a habit, after every visit that I made to the Balkans, both in the Bosnian war and in the Kosovo war to submit a private report to the Prime Minister, which was not published, and which carried my impressions and recommendations. That report was in no way a political instrument. It was a private report, as we return to the word "loyal," as a British subject to his Prime Minister about what is happening, and my report submitted after this. I don't have it immediately handy would have reflected these facts. Can I also say for fear that you think that this is being done for as it were electoral political purposes, that at this voice -- at this time, I was a completely lone voice calling for greater action in Bosnia? My repeated attempts to drag Bosnia on to the public scene in Britain were hugely derided. I was a loan voice not only in the House of Commons where I was booed and shouted at when I tried to raise these matters but I was very nearly a loan voice even in my own party on the matter. So I think -- I think that the claim that this would have been done for political purposes does not accord with my recollection of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I must say it's a bit frustrating how you are able to know where I'm going next with my question and answer the question before I ask it.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to be unhelpful to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's helpful it's just that you're getting there before I do. I think it's fair to say that you were frustrated by the inaction of John Major and that were you trying to goad him into some kind of action by making a public case about this matter?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I was trying to goad not only him I was trying to goad the entire western powers who sat by and did nothing while this happened or at least not enough, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall a time where he became sufficiently frustrated by your efforts in that regard that he accused you of "having done nothing but grandstand on this issue from the commencement of the matter? If he really understood a little more about it he might say a little less about it." Do you recall him saying that about you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Many years later I do recall in the heat of exchanges in the House of Commons when I may have goaded him I think on the issue of, if I recall, of Kakanj power station outside Sarajevo, he said those words. I don't think anybody would say that every word said in the heat of the exchanges in the House of Commons are ones that people would stand by later on and indeed John Major has been generous enough, it's part of his personality, to acknowledge later on, that what we were seeking to do, what I was seeking to do at the time, was something which turned out to be the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to talk about this -- this issue of exaggeration that we've been talking about. We were talking about it a little earlier -- in a little more detail. At one point you made this statement, "I stress that these claims," referring to claims of people you had talked to, "Are claims in a war that is thick with claims and exaggeration." And I take it that when you make that statement you are basing it on a pattern of things that you were told which you learned later were exaggerations?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: In all wars there are exaggerations and in this these wars I think there as many as any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case though that the Balkans tends to be a bit unique about this sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I really don't think the Balkans is unique when it comes to over exaggerating what happens in war. It happens there as much but no more than anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume you've read Lord Owen's book Balkan Odyssey?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Do you want me to be honest Mr. Ackerman? I got a few pages into it but found it wasn't very compelling reading after a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think only a Lord could say that about another Lord, perhaps. But in any event, he said -- if you got a little ways into it you at least got through the introduction. And in the introduction he said this with regard to his experiences there, and I'm just going to ask you if you agree with him. "Never before, in over 30 years of public life, have I had to operate in such a climate of dishonour, propaganda, and dissembling. Many of the people with whom I have had to deal in the former Yugoslavia were literally strangers to the truth."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Do I agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I have disagreed with Lord Owen about many things and many of them about the Balkans. I disagree with the blanket nature of that statement, yes, thoroughly disagree with it. There are honourable decent, truthful courageous people of all ethnicities in the Balkans and that statement seems to deny the existence of such people who I meet every single day I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also in your letter to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please keep the interpreters in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we will keep the interpreters in mind, we are being told to keep the interpreters in mind so we must go slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your letter to General Nambiar, you referred to this again. You said this to him. "There are stories from the Serb side" I better tell you where I am. I am on page 2 the second paragraph. "There are stories from the Serb side of the bodies of their own people being floated, tied together, past their own positions and of the cries of their people being tortured in the night. There are similar blood curdling tales of Serbian atrocities to Muslims in Gorazde, which I heard from Muslims on their side in Sarajevo. As you will know as well as any, war is a great manufacturer of exaggeration and this one is certainly no exception." True?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, let me tell you this: That I don't think even in our wildest imagination decent people like you and I could have believed that some of the things that we now know went on in these camps, in this war, on all sides, went on. I think it is the reaction of the decent ordinary person brought up in a civilised society to believe these tales when they are told must be exaggerations because no human beings could reduce themselves to such deprivation, but I think any one of us who dismisses all the tales we have heard in the light of the evidence that we now know went on in Omarska, Keraterm, and elsewhere as mere exaggerations must now be a judgement that they would reconsider. I certainly do. I do not claim that every story -- I do not claim that every story that we hear is correct. I do, however, say that some of those things that decent people thought must be exaggeration we now know to have been the truth but we said they were exaggeration because they were beyond our imaginings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we come together, you and I, there pretty closely, I think. I've been here since 1997 looking at these cases, trying these cases, and of course it's true that many of the claims that are made are absolutely the case and they are in many cases revolting. That doesn't remove from one's consideration, however, what you correctly observe when you were there, and that is in any kind of a war situation, the exaggerations go on. The concern that I have and one that I'm sure you also share is to what extent that culture, that tendency, permeates into the courtrooms of this Tribunal and that's why I ask you that question?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think it's a perfectly fair question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not at all sure, forgive me Lord Ashdown, that it is, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd say it's more of a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The point I was trying to make is that the language I use here is not the language I use in this courtroom it's the language I recorded in my diary at the time. These are my objective observations and I think it is fair to say that anybody reading these diaries might conclude not least from the passages we have had our attention drawn to by Mr. Ackerman that I was making an attempt to be objective and not to exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope you didn't hear me accusing you of engaging in exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I didn't but I understand the reason why Ms. Korner intruded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well you and I thought the question was appropriate if no one else did. Isn't it your experience, which is broad and -- that people, that human beings, once having made a claim that may very well be exaggerated and untrue have a very hard time backing off of that claim?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No doubt that's a human failing. It's also my experience that I recall very well, as no doubt you do, Mr. Ackerman, that when the first stories of Auschwitz and Belsen came out they were put down as exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to your letter to the Prime Minister now. Another thing you told the Prime Minister about the people you talked to, in addition to the deprivation of Serb extremists at night was also this, I'm on page 3, the first paragraph, last sentence: "They were also under pressure from Muslim extremists who wish to recruit them for fighting." I assume they told you that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally, you tell the Prime Minister this: "You could also keep the men away from the clutches of the extremists of one side who terrorise and those of the other who are seeking to radicalise and recruit them, the Muslims in Bosnia are not religious extremists but they are fast being radicalised. If we fail to act then we should realise that we are creating in these wretched camps, Europe's Palestinians of the future." And that was in connection with your effort to get the Prime Minister to, on his own, in cooperation with other interested states, to establish safe havens where these people could be protected not only from Serbs but from their own people?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Obviously correct. I mean the -- if the point you're seeking to make or wanting me to confirm is that there were extremists on all sides I readily confirm it. If the point you are seeking to establish is that it would have been better to have taken certain areas out of the combat in which non-combatants can be secured I readily confirm it. If the point you're seeking to make is that is somehow or another those who I saw, saw an equivalence between their own people whether extreme or not and the Serbs then I reject it completely. If they had to be anywhere they would have preferred to be in the hands of their own extremists than in the hands of the Serbs, who had done them such terrible torture and damage in the camps from which they had come and I suspect in Manjaca before I got there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your letter to Sommaruga, ICRC, like your letter to Dr. Karadzic, was urging an early exchange of prisoners. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say this on page 3, "Dr. Karadzic tells me that the Muslim authorities refused to exchange prisoners and are even in some places demanding a rifle, a box of ammunition and a sack of flour from the Serb authorities for every exchanged prisoner." Were you ever able to verify this as to whether what Dr. Karadzic had told you was correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. That was Dr. Karadzic's claim. Let we underline the word "claim." And as you will see in the next sentence to Mr. Sommaruga I ask him if this is correct. I didn't receive a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my next question. Did you receive a reply to any of these letters, a written reply?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I did receive a reply from John Major, though I -- I don't have that available. From my memory it would have been the kind of reply which a government minister sends to a member of the opposition, where they don't want to do what the member of the opposition is asking and would have contained I suspect no evidence of interest to this Court. As regards Cornelio Sommaruga, Dr. Karadzic, and General Nambiar, no, not as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In addition to your diary and your letters in connection with the materials we were supplied, we were supplied a number of articles, newspaper articles or something of that nature. Do you have any idea what I'm talking about when I talk about those?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I recall one article that I wrote after this. In fact it wasn't an article at all, one newspaper simply reprinted the letter I wrote to Mr. Major, the guardian newspaper, as I recall. I -- my memory is not as good as it should be. I cannot remember any other articles I wrote at the time but if you have them available I certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This isn't one you wrote but it is one you are apparently quoted in. And what I'll do is I'll have the usher hand it to you and put it on the ELMO and then we can all see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the ERN number, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I -- look at it and see if you recognise it at all but the part I'm interested in is where it says, "Bradley, I believe that Geneva Convention is being upheld and from what I can tell, it is being followed to the absolute limits that it is possible to do." Do you have any idea where that came from? Are you actually referring to someone named Bradley?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I presume so. It just, however, might mean "broadly." I must say, it does seem to me a -- Mr. Ackerman, this is ten years ago, I regret I just can't provide you with a veracity or otherwise of this report, though there are some things in it which even at that stage I would have known to have been inaccurate but -- I mean to refer to people as the Muslim Slavs and et cetera doesn't seem to me to be the kind of phrase that anybody who knew the situation would have used at that stage. This looks to me like an excerpt from the interview which I gave to the Banja Luka TV which has been previously commented upon but without knowing this I'm afraid I can't help very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you'll notice at the top the story is an united press international story, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed but without knowing its provenance I simply can't help you with this. I have a suspicion that this is a -- a -- a lifted sentence from that Banja Luka TV interview, and the difference in the wordings between the two may well be ascribed to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, are you going to tender this document as an exhibit? Because it does not actually form part of attachment 8 and goes beyond the enumeration of attachment 8 so if you're going -- if you think it's important enough to tender it into the records as an exhibit please go ahead. If not we'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your career, you've given a lot of interviews. You've been quoted a lot. And I dare say you've been misquoted a lot?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I certainly have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not something that a person in your position is a stranger to, the business of being misquoted in print. Correct? And even by journalists we would consider responsible journalists, correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Journalists have a very tough job to do, sometimes at very fast speed and in difficult conditions and that applies most especially to journalists covering a war. I don't think any of them would claim that everything they had written was perfect or even in the light of events, necessarily totally accurate but what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And sometimes they will agree that they may have misquoted you and other times they will contend rather vociferously that they did not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: More frequently the latter than the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Have you found since in the times that you've been spending in Bosnia, and certainly been frequent lately, do you find that you're more frequently misquoted when there is a translation involved? Or have you paid any attention to that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think it's more -- I think it's more frequent most frequent of all that your quotes though accurate are taken out of context. And I think that is more often the case than a deliberate or mistaken misquotation but certainly, the translation question provides a greater opportunity for the misunderstanding, misuse of words, without any malice intended it's just the process. Our languages don't perfectly match.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to try to find this now. 02195568 is the page and again I'll ask the usher to -- unfortunately I've written on it. Okay. This is another article it's a daily report from the foreign broadcast information service, which I'm not familiar with but you probably are. And it deals with an interview or a statement or something that you said. Speaking about your visit to Bosnia and your visit to the camps, it reports that you said that Muslims had in fact found refuge in the camps and also protection from local -- I don't know whether it's local extremists it's hard to see because I can't --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It's local extremists, I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you go on to say -- you don't go on to say, the article goes on to say the British delegation did not venture to visit Gorazde because the United Nations protection force could not guarantee safety. Gorazde is a town in southeastern Bosnia-Herzegovina held by Muslims. So the situation that you encountered in August in Bosnia was that Republika Srpska, where Manjaca and Trnopolje were located, were safe for you to visit but Gorazde, where Serbs were held by Muslims under conditions that may not have been all that satisfactory, was not safe for you to visit? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It is, but you need to know why it's a fair statement. In any area fully in the control of any one of the ethnicities, you could during the Bosnian war reasonably safely visit. In other words, if I was going into a Bosniak area which was behind the front line, or a Croat area Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. behind the front line or a Serb area behind the front line, the authorities who dominated that would provide you with a degree of safety which you would go in, not totally without risk. A wholly different situation, however, from moving into a front line area. Manjaca was not a front line area. Trnopolje was a refugee gathering point, a displaced persons gathering point, miles from the front line. Self-evidently that's a safer area than going to Gorazde which was a front line area and incidentally, the point you presume about Gorazde, Mr. Ackerman, is not entirely correct. The people who were being besieged in Gorazde were the Bosnians, they were the Muslims, the people who were doing the besieging were the Serbs. So Gorazde was held by Muslims in -- the same Muslims - if we call them that - in the same way as Sarajevo was. But around Gorazde was a Serb siege and constant fighting. Indeed, the situation was even more complex than that. Gorazde at this time was like a doughnut, there was a ring of Serbs encompassing a ring of Muslims encompassing a ring of Serbs, around a centre held by the Muslims. There was constant fighting going on. This was the front line. It was an immensely more dangerous place for obvious reasons which I'm sure you'll understand as an ex-soldier than moving into a rear area such as Manjaca and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last sentence, Ashdown added it was necessary to unblock Gorazde and try to release the Serbs who are being held captive there.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: That's correct but that's the description I just provided to you. If you look at the letter to General Nambiar you'll see a better description of what this comes from. In that letter, I say surely the means of unlocking the problem in Gorazde is to unlock the Muslim siege of the Serb outer ring by moving the Serbs out. You would have then have created a complete Muslim area albeit still circled by Serbs who could then have become a safe area and indeed that is exactly what happened. What happened subsequently you will recall Mr. Ackerman, was that there were three so-called safe havens, Zepce, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. So what I was proposing was a means by which as it were the inner ring of Serb surrounders could be released creating a Muslim area, which could then become a safe haven and could then move towards a resolution of the problem. Does that make the matter clearer to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm through with that document now and I don't need to make it an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told Ms. Korner I would let her know about my progress. It's my estimate that I have about another 20 minutes which means I'll go for about ten or 15 minutes after the break, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I don't think it's worth starting the next witness until Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well Your Honour, as I say I need to explain the witness problems we have so I don't think we need as it were bust a gut over this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What do you prefer, Mr. Ackerman, stop now and take the full 20 minutes after the break or have ten minutes now and then continue with a further ten minutes after the break? I would -- I would dare suggest, if I have the indulgence of the interpreters and if we could possibly go beyond the time that we are allocated before we usually have a break by a further ten minutes and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I've got various matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will have a break and in the meantime Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see what you mean sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would the technicians and the interpreters agree to that? In other words, we proceed for another 20 minutes from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Judge, that's an estimate. I'm not going to guarantee I'll finish in 20 minutes. I think I will.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If possible, the interpreters would prefer to take their break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the suggestion that I have is that we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can I suggest to you to shorten it to 20 minutes rather than 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for just a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back to your diary, Monday, 10 August, the time you were in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 02 -- it's actually page 11, the circled number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 5554.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Pale was the head of the -- the headquarters of the government of Republika Srpska at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And also the headquarters of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I don't know about the headquarters of the SDS party but I can certainly confirm it was Karadzic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And what you said about Pale in the first paragraph of that report was, "Pale is a town where apparently --"

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: You'll have to direct me to this in which paragraph are we in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Under the 10th of August, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it starts with "up at six."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Got you, right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's in the middle of that paragraph, "Pale is a town where apparently Muslims are allowed still to live but there is no sign here that they have been subject to any shelling or the kind of deprivations which Sarajevo was subjected to." True?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes, but the two sentences need to be disconnected. Pale is a town where apparently Muslims are allowed still to live. Let me just say to you, Mr. Ackerman, if I may, that apparently means that that's what I was informed, I saw no Muslims living there. Let me also say to you that this would have come directly from my conversations to Mr. -- with Mr. Karadzic. Now I must say to you that of all the people I've met in my life Mr. Karadzic was able to lie to you straight to your face in a way more convincing than any other man I've met. A fact that I discovered later. The second sentence refers to Pale as a whole, in other words, the generality of the people showed no signs of suffering either the shelling or the deprivation than ordinary people Muslim, Serb, and Croat included in Sarajevo, so the two sentences are not connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't see any burned out residence or residences or things of that nature, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I can recall seeing no significant destruction in Pale of the sort that I found elsewhere but on the other hand I can also recall never seeing any Muslims living there although I was told that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked earlier today about your conception of the Serb forces. You talked about how well the leather was kept on the uniforms, how they seemed to be extremely well organised, all of that. And one of the things that you spoke about with regard to that was the time you spent with the royal marines and how that gave you military training and knowledge with which you could fairly effectively judge the effectiveness of a force by observing them?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you once say this with regard to the Serb forces? And you're speaking of your government. "The massive misjudgement that the government is making is that these people, being the Serb forces are not the IRA, they are not the Vietnamese, I've watch these people, they are local town thugs, they are not trained, they are not fit, they are not prepared to close with the enemy, they run whenever somebody actually fires back at them, they are cowards, most of them." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I do recall saying, you'll have to quote the precise -- but I certainly said things like that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're familiar with the book written by a fellow Simms, it was published recently, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: You mean, "The Unfinest Hour"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you've read that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I've read bits of it, yes. Including the bits that refer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to talk about some of those. He says that your stance on the Bosnian war was confused and inconsistent?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I wonder if I could do you the favour of stopping you there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Could I invite you to look at the latest version of that book which perhaps you haven't seen? In the forward in which Mr. Simms gives me a very handsome apology for completely misjudging the statements he made in the previous book and I have indeed letters to that effect which he has kindly sent me in the last few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the one I have probably is not the latest addition of that book?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It is rare indeed for a journalist, for an author to show such generosity but if you would draw your attention to the book I think published about two weeks ago, in which he offers me a very handsome apology for completely misjudging both my actions and my intentions in that. I could quote that to you if you wish but I suspect it may not help your case, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Lord Ashdown and Mr. Ackerman please slow down and allow a short interval of time between the question and answer again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've left me now with no choice but to basically bring to your attention the things that are published in the book and ask you if these are things that he has disavowed or not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I can assure that you he's disavowed that whole piece and if you wish, Mr. -- Your Honour, I can ask for a latest copy of the book to be brought together with the letter that he has written me in the last two weeks, in most handsome manner, and generous manner completely altering that opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner can take care of that after consulting you later on. That would be useful once this matter has been brought up and answered in the way that Lord Ashdown has. I think it's important that we have the -- at least the clarification that has been made. I mean not necessarily the entire latest edition of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The preface would do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. Ackerman is going to pursue this line we will certainly make arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Ackerman is going to pursue it or not that's his business.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the moment I'm not altogether clear what the author's opinions about Mr. Ashdown's views are of any relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They could be of relevance, of course they could be, but at this point in time, I think taking into consideration the way Lord Ashdown has butted in, stopping reasonably so I would say, Mr. Ackerman from proceeding further at that point in time, I don't know what Mr. Ackerman intends doing but perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Neither does Mr. Ackerman, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon? Perhaps you could move to something different, Mr. Ackerman, I don't know. I'm not making suggestions to you but at this point in time I think that would be wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem with what you've told me, Lord Ashdown, is that many places when he speaks of you, he cites to various publications that he is quoting from and I take it that he's certainly not in a position to disavow what is contained in those publications?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think that's fair, Your Honour. It's his conclusions that he's disavowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For instance, the quote that we talked about, the massive misjudgement, the government is making, is that these people are not the IRA, they are not the Vietnamese, I've watched these people, they are local town thug, they are not trained, they are not fit, they are not prepared to close with the enemy, they run when somebody actually fires back at them, they are cowards, most of them, is attributed to Anthony Bevins who is fairly well known, an article British military intervention in Bosnia ruled out, an article from The Independent of, I think, 4 December, 1992, if that's the -- the question is, did you actually make that statement?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: If that's quoted in -- Anthony Bevins, who is a highly respected journalist I would certainly have made that statement. I don't deny that fact for a moment but let me point out to you, Mr. Ackerman, the fact that the composition of the Serb army was a core army largely drawn from the JNA. Those are people I would have seen as I moved around Bosnia in the description given in my diaries, supported by irregulars, the most famous of which was Mr. Vojislav Seselj's Tigers, who operated in manners which many of the Yugoslav professional soldiers found distasteful and operated in the manners I've described there but not I believe without command and control. So what I'm referring to there is the Serb irregulars, who on this visit I did not see but on subsequent visits I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next one that I draw your attention to is this: And I'm on page 296 of the book now. Referring to another one of your positions. You're quoted as saying, "This is a war of minorities, they are all Serb Croat, Muslims, Orthodox, or Catholic national minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina which may help to explain why they exercised a local majority they enjoy with such ferocity." Would you agree that you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: If that's in quotation marks, I have no reason to believe I didn't make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, according to the note, it's actually from an article you wrote, we are making Europe's Palestinians, published in The Independent?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: And date, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the 13th of August, 1992. So that would have been right after you came back?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: And reflects the statement that I put into -- into the Major letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the next quote, same page, same paragraph, I'll tell you where this one comes from, it comes from something called Hansard, which I'm not familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Hansard is the record of parliamentary proceedings and always accurate, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. He says in April 1993, he, you, made the extraordinary claim that even if the Serbs were now the principal offenders a powerful case can be made that the aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina was started by the Muslims as much as by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I have never ascribed to any party the monopoly of either aggression or of -- or of atrocity. I've always said that dark and unacceptable acts took place on both sides but I have no doubt where the weight of aggression came from. It came from the Serb side and I have no doubt where by far the preponderance of the atrocities came from, it came from the Serb side. If your point is to say were there Muslim units capable of acting in an inappropriate and illegal way of course there were. Some of them have been tried here. I can only report in this what I saw and the conditions of Manjaca at the time and I report that as accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Lord Ashdown, the interpreters would like to you slow down and so would I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked earlier I'm going to go back to some of your testimony when Ms. Korner was questioning you. You were talking about your trip from Pale to Banja Luka by way of Brcko through what you say has become known as the Posavina corridor and the destruction of houses, buildings. You know that what was going on there was some pretty heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was actually a war going on there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And much of what the destruction you saw was a result of artillery fire from across the border from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Perfectly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Let me point out, however, not that I think you need me to that of course in front line areas great destruction is going to take place. That does not reply to the rear areas which I describe in places like Kozarac, the neighbourhood -- in the neighbourhood of Omarska, Keraterm, and Manjaca. Those places had never seen front line fighting. Those were civilian populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look again at Exhibit P405. Now you've seen this document earlier today. It's apparently an order from the 1st Krajina Corps command which talks about -- of 3 August, 1992, talking about the visit of the international committee to the detention committees at Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor. And this second paragraph, it says, and we've all -- already dealt with this today but let's do it again, "In this regard all measures are to be taken to make conditions in these camps satisfactory. This implies, order, cleanliness, functional medical care for the detainees" and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Several questions. First of all this is a fairly strong indication, is it not that each of those facilities was under the control of the military?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It is both that and an implication that such order and cleanliness had not existed beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Secondly, when you were at Manjaca, I take it no one told you that there had been a massive cleanup and fix-up and change-up over the last two or will three days?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It was implied in what the prisoners had said to me that things were improving remarkably over the recent period and it was that improvement that I wished to see continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thirdly, I don't know if your experience in the military is like mine but I have a hunch that it is. In the American army we had inspections called IG inspections, inspector general inspections. And before those were to happen, there would be an order fairly similar to this and there would be a flurry of activity, cleaning, ordering, all kinds of things, before the inspector general showed up to look at our facility.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I suspect this is nothing to do with inspector generals and I'm sure you do too, Mr. Ackerman this is to do with the fact that the International Red Cross was coming around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It also had to do with the fact that someone was coming to visit the camp and they wanted it to be in as good condition as it could be in for that visit?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I think that's a fair implication but let's remember who it was who was coming to visit the camp it was not the regular Serb military authorities it was the international community that was coming, your presumption that this would have been the normal course of events for a regular visit by the Serbs does not from my point of view seem to be borne out. It looks to me as though this is a cleanup ahead of an exceptional and unwelcome visit by an international -- by the international committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect, though, don't you -- and don't you agree that if there was going to be some kind of an official visit by the commanding general, that there would probably also be some kind of a fix up, clean up, get ready?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Your presumption Mr. Ackerman is that ever been a visit by the commanding general I think that's a dangerous assumption to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there ever was.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Or indeed ever intended to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that leads me actually to -- we are getting yelled at for overlapping now. Okay. That leads me actually to my next question. You have no knowledge, do you about when the authorities that you visited in Pale, Mr. Karadzic and people associated with him, first became aware of actual conditions at places like Manjaca, Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I have no knowledge -- I have no knowledge. I can speculate, if you -- if that's helpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd prefer you not speculate?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: But I suspect that this matter became -- came an urgent political matter when it was revealed by the international press that does not mean that it was not known of beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the opposite could also be true, that that's when it was first learned about?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: In the realms of speculation, Mr. Ackerman, any of these speculations could be true. I know which one I would prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The same could be true with regard to the authorities in Banja Luka, I take it. With the possible exception of the military authorities that might have been in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Self-evidently, it's perfectly possible, though everything that I know about the Balkans and that war makes it seem to me highly unlikely that this was not known by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at P1128-24 again, please. It's a photograph. You looked at this photograph earlier today and I'm confused as to which person you believed was which. There is a person on the left with a mustache and then a person on the right, and one of them you referred to as a military man. Which one would that be?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The one on the left, and as my memory recalls, this is reaching back over ten years, so I suppose the Court should not put a huge amount of weight on this but as I recall, this was the man amongst whom -- he was amongst those military people I met in Manjaca on the night before I went in there. On the afternoon that I went in there. The man on the right, as I recall it, was the man who -- one of the two people, I think the one I'm more doubtful about, about whose appearance I'm more doubtful in my diary that I met at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recognised the insignia on the man on the left as we look at the picture with the mustache?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: To be honest I don't but judging by the two bars I would imagine he was -- I don't know the insignias of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that that's a U.S. Army --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: If it was a U.S. Army it would be a Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a U.S. Army patch?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: So it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is for a specialist six, enlisted?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: On matters related to the U.S. Army, Mr. Ackerman, I concede your expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. I'm finished with that. In your direct testimony, you said that while you were at Trnopolje, you saw people walking the lanes leading toward Trnopolje who had clearly been ordered to go there. Are you saying you could tell by the way they were walking that they had been ordered to go there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, certainly not, but I think it's a fair presumption, given that they were not under escort from the military or the police, and given that they were heading towards this place which was a hell hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that people went there absolutely voluntarily in the hopes of catching a convoy to get out of that area?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
