utterances.text: I think it's entirely likely that having been burnt, brutalised, raped and shot out of their houses they would have accepted instructions to go to an area from which they were told they would be transported to freedom. Frankly, in those circumstances, if I had been so instructed, I probably would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you accept that as bad as Trnopolje was, that it may have been a safer place than outside Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I certainly do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the communities outside Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, I certainly do not. Whether you call being burnt out of your house, having your husband killed, and being told to go to a place and then going there, going there voluntarily is a matter for to you decide on. But it is perfectly possible and regrettably it happened frequently and on all sides that people were informed that if they went to a certain place they would find safety, to find out that when they got there they found terror. Let me remind you, if I may, Mr. Ackerman, that the people I saw at Trnopolje that day who were then taken away and tipped over the cliffs, to Vlasic two or three days later and their faces will haunt me were told that they were being moved to Travnik to be handed over to their own kit and kin, the Muslims but they weren't. In much the same way I have no doubt that the people who were driven from their houses and told to go to Trnopolje could well have been told that they were going there to be moved to safer -- because it was safer when they discovered had they got there, sorry, when they got there they discovered something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that thousands of people were actually transported from Trnopolje to relative safety?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I am not at all surprised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the remarkable film that was produced by ITN that day, the authorities were required and indeed did respond to international pressure to make sure that people were finally moved to safety but I deeply regret and I often torture myself with the thought that those who I saw did not receive such a happy fate and I often wonder if I'd have done something different, if I'd have stayed in those camps rather than returning to Belgrade whether that outcome might have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But even before the press went there, even before you went there, don't you know that thousands of people had been transported out of there to Travnik and other Croatia, other places of safety?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I don't know that. If there is evidence to prove that I would accept that but the word thousands strikes me as being extraordinary. But Mr. Ackerman, however many may have been transported out of there, the fact is that many more or at least many were taken away from there to their deaths. They were civilians, they were women, they were children, they were the elderly, they were the infirm and when I saw them, they were living under conditions which were indescribable, unimaginable, and impossible to exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Many times in your letters and diaries, you have spoken about the Serb people that were making an effort to protect the people there in Trnopolje from the extremists that were running around the country?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's why I asked you, don't you think they may have been at least during those moments, safer there than if they had been out in the country where those extremists were running --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I'm sure if you had asked any one of them would you prefer to have been in this place or out of it they would have preferred to be out of it. Let me just say this, I have a great admiration for the Serb people. They are brave, honourable, they suffer from amongst their populations in probably the same proportions as we suffer in ours from psychopaths and killers and when they get in charge they can do impossible things, unbelievable things, but the actions of the Serbs in so far as they are true as told me, the local Serbs in seeking to protect these people from the depredations of the irregular gangs we spoke of earlier on was an extremely brave act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that it was an open camp that people could go in and out of pretty much as will?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: A point that is made in my diary. When you say go in and out of pretty much at will I think every person there would have recognised that if they had left that camp and been found they would have been returned to the camp but yes there was passage in and out of the camp. In much the same way there was in the gulags of the archipelago -- of Soviet Russia. There were no fences around those but people knew leaving those camps would have ended up in them being returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that they were going out in the daytime to forage for food, to dig in the gardens, to find food in the houses, and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I am completely unsurprised given that they were given no food while they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another question, another issue. When you gave your interview to Banja Luka TV, the evening after you had returned from Manjaca, that I take it was also done through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it the same interpreter that had been with you at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Ackerman, I simply can't remember. If I recall, it wasn't. I think it was in fact the interpreter -- either the interpreter from The Financial Times who I referred to earlier on or it may indeed have been the interpreter who came with the -- with the television interviewer. It's more normal for an interpreter to come with the television interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could the other microphone please be turned on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No I think we got it. Let me ask you this, and you may or may not agree with me. Have you made the observation that there seems to be a kind of cultural natural law in the Balkans, and I think you know what I mean when I say "natural law" that goes like this? It is seen to be legal and appropriate to do to others what they have done to you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I don't think you have to be in the Balkans to have such a law, Mr. Ackerman. An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth is a well known saying and human emotion. Right across the world. But as I think we all recognised in civilised society that's an emotion you should seek to resist. Let me just say if you are trying to make the point that the Balkans were a place of exceptional killing and exceptional unpleasant practices I think we in Europe need to perhaps with some humility recognise that these peoples more than anybody else who over a thousand years have slaughtered themselves in revenge and nationalism and about borders and numbers which are simply incalculable and more than any other nation have no right to say that the Balkans is exceptional in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You couldn't be more right about that.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: The point I make Mr. Ackerman if I may is that we have learned that we have to find different standards and the same applies to the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were in Manjaca, you told us that the people you were most interested in were the people that had just arrived there from the Omarska and Keraterm facilities. And that you spent very little time looking at, talking with, learning anything from, those that had been there a longer time. You did make the observation, I'm sure, that those that had been there a longer time, who had not just arrived there, appeared to be in a great deal better shape?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: It would be scarcely possible to be in a worse shape without being dead than the people from Omarska. That does not mean to say that the others were in a shape that you would have found to be humanly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally, two questions: During any of the times you visited Bosnia in 1992, did you ever meet with or speak with Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Radoslav?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I cannot recall the names of all those to whom I met and spoke Mr. Ackerman but certainly the name doesn't spring out at me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you to your recollection that if you wanted to do a certain thing you would have to meet with or talk with Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: No, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, as you sit here now, that the person who is accused in this case is named Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there a re-examination, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one question arising out of that Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that your permission to visit this area and these camps came directly from Dr. Karadzic himself?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Indeed. And it was only the use of his name and that authority which got me past the opposition of the local soldiers, in order to visit the camp. They accepted the authority of their president.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, did you have to go and talk to any of the as it were, the politicians in the area in which you were?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Not that I recall. There may have been members of the political nomenclature amongst those whom I met in Banja Luka when I was trying to seek entry into Manjaca but I do not recall them being identified as politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one question: This authorisation that you had from Dr. Karadzic himself, I understood it was a verbal one?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How could you communicate it to the authorities of the various camps that you visited?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN
utterances.text: Because I had interpreters with me. It was remarkable, Your Honour, because as we passed through the battle areas around Brcko and leading up to Brcko and through the Posavina corridor, on every road block that we were stopped at, the driver and the interpreter said to the people who were manning the road block that Karadzic had given me permission to pass and that was sufficient to allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Okay. That brings us to the end of your testimony, Lord Ashdown. I thank you on behalf of my two colleagues and on behalf of the Tribunal for having accepted to come and give evidence in this trial. Also, knowing what a tight schedule you have. Thank you for finding us a slot. You will be escorted now by the usher and attended to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Gustin will actually go out because there is some people he has to talk to before leaving the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you start, Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Halilovic. Our decision which is going to be an oral one is that going through the taped transcripts, we believe that there is a matter that ought to be disclosed. If you prefer to have details, we would hand out details. We have identified in the various tapes and on various parts --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware Your Honour had any tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You haven't had those either. All we gave you was a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the summary you did refer to tapes and page numbers and this is what I'm referring to. And therefore our decision is that the material that you referred to ought to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which? I mean I think Your Honour will have -- indicate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a list of the pages. I think what we ought to do is we will hand out all the pages that you indicated to us from tape 1, starting on tape 1 and then going to other tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm just wondering whether or not we are at cross-purposes here. Can I see the document Your Honour is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it downstairs in my office. Do you have a copy of it here? Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just check because I'm slightly confused by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically we are talking of tape 1, page 17, where -- in which Mr. Izetbegovic is alleged to have made a statement, and he is supposedly quoted verbatim. Then there is tape 4, part 1, page 9, regarding the Green Berets, and about the establishment in Stari Gradiska area. Tape 8, part 2, page 8, the importation of Bujadin [phoen] to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that certain Alija Izetbegovic would be in charge of terrorist group known as Sevel [phoen] or however you pronounce it. And then there is tape 25, part 1, page 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I have a look at the document for a moment, I'm very sorry, I didn't bring it I didn't know Your Honour was going to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want we can hand down a detailed decision as to what we think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I think I would like it's not so much that I would like I'm pretty certain that those who have the conduct of this particular case would want to have reasons in writing why it needs to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I continue, tape 13, about the patriotic league, tape 2, part 1, about smuggling of weapons, even though does not seem to refer -- specifically to the ARK region. And then finally tape 3

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may I put a halt to this at the moment? I think we'd like a written decision, please, reasons for disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will prepare one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But be prepared in other words knowing beforehand that our decision is that there is Rule 68 material which ought to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hear what Your Honour says but I think weighed like the reasons why Your Honours think it's Rule 68, it's not for us for those who have the conduct of the case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be done. It may take a couple of days but it will be done. So problems with your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have no witness for Monday, full stop. I'm afraid. Your Honour, I am going to ask, we haven't actually been yet offered the list of dates for next year. In other words when we are going to be sitting and when we are not going to be sitting. I am very anxious that -- clearly my anxiety is that we sit as much as possible but that if there are to be breaks, they are decided breaks in advance about which we know so that we do not go through what we went through this month over the changes, non-changes, and reverse changes. As a result, I regret to tell Your Honours that we cannot get the witness here for Monday. We have witnesses on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday. I'll give Your Honours the numbers, 7.3 on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. 7.3, Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.228 on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.134 on Thursday. And on Friday, 7.54, who is a new witness and he'll be called in full. In other words, when I say a new witness, he's not somebody who has testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you confident that indeed between Tuesday and Thursday, you will conclude with those three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I was about to tell Your Honour we think it's unlikely we will be sitting a full session on any of those dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, are you confident that we will conclude with the witness we had scheduled for today, do you think we will conclude with him on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if not, he will go into Monday and that will fill Monday up because we don't have anybody else. Your Honour at the moment then for after the Christmas break, we have started witnesses on the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And witness 7.46 will be the second witness, and he's likely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.46. If Your Honour -- I can give Your Honours we have estimated 7.179 for the Monday, because he's testified before in Stakic, 7.46, although he testified in Tadic, I'm going to be calling him in full because it's Tadic testimony is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you intending to start that witness on Monday the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No that will be the Tuesday. And then we have 7.43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate that witness will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Including cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very difficult to say but he will certainly be a full day, I would imagine, in chief, and I can't say about cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But what I'm -- the reason I raise this business of having a schedule and sticking to it is I'm aware that that week of course is the Serb Orthodox or the Orthodox new year, now are we having a day off for that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think we have to be reasonable now. I will be -- we will be not -- we will not be sitting for the Serb Christmas but I think we need to go ahead then. I mean I think it's reasonable. I'm pretty sure that your client will not take this as an affront or as lack of respect to his -- to his religion. So my intention is to proceed. And then between now and when we pack up for our Christmas holidays, we will discuss the January, February, March schedule. I am still waiting for a confirmation from the bureau as to the dates when each Chamber is sitting. I will verify with my secretary whether that has been concluded. We can take it up from there but my intention is to work hard and give you enough space to ensure that you finish your case --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm very keen and at the rate we are going, unless we sit full time effectively, between January the 13th and Easter, which I believe is in April sometime next year, we won't finish before Easter and I think we really should aim to try to finish by Easter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another thing is there anyway in which we could utilise Monday even short of having a witness present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I hesitate to suggest it but one thing that hasn't happened. I won't be here next week but the one thing that hasn't happened is we've hardly looked at a single document from the Prijedor -- because we have not been able to call the witnesses in full to go through the documents. Although we are actually arranging because of this problem that there will be a summary done of each of the documents as to what it relates to, which we will provide, nonetheless, if Your Honours were minded to at least go through or allow the Prosecution to take Your Honours through some of the documents, particularly relating to the background in Prijedor because we've not really heard about any of them. But that's afraid the only thing I can suggest at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It won't surprise you that I would object very strongly to that. It's my contention that that process is in the nature of a submission and an improper submission, and providing you with summaries of those documents is absolutely a submission and I think it's totally improper and I would object to that being done. I trust Your Honours to read the documents. When I start putting in documents, I'll trust to you read mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do read them, we assure you, even though we are literally fighting against time to be able to read the bulk that we have. Ms. Korner, with regard to Halilovic, at this point in time, if you have the transcripts to which the summary that you had handed to us earlier available, readily available, we would like to have them as soon as possible so that our written decision will incorporate textual --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want all the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what we require is the taped transcripts relating to the parts of tapes 1, 4, 8, 25, 13, 2 and 3. I will leave you one of my -- one of our legal officers will hand down to you the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you give us the parts that you consider are rule 68, of which I say I'm a little surprised as you may have gathered, then we'll get the transcripts available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's important so that we go into some details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it would assist. Your Honour will recall we've had this discussion sometimes more heated than others about what is Rule 68 but I think it would help us and probably would help Mr. Ackerman as well if you could identify in your ruling why you say this is Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean but it's doesn't take much for example. If there is an allegation that, by the Defence, that there was such a thing as the Patriotic League and that it was active --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we are not denying that there was a Patriotic League so why is it Rule 68. If we were saying there was no such thing then I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because together with it there are references with regard to the activities of mujahedin and also what is alleged to have been state terrorism activated and maintained by a certain Mr. Izetbegovic. How do you expect that not to be -- not to fall under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's Your Honour, I think that's it's the dates that -- as I recall all this stuff but I'll have a look again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This mujahedin and terrorist business we are talking of actually May, 1992, from the details that I have collected. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this just makes me extremely nervous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before -- before I have expressed my concern that Ms. Korner does not understand what Rule 68 is and it's been confirmed again today and I just have this fear that there is this huge amount of Rule 68 material out there that she doesn't think is Rule 68 but which all the rest of us would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not talk on things that we are not sure of or that we cannot prove. When you brought up the subject, Ms. Korner was the first one to stand up and admit that there had been a shortcoming which she was very much prepared to make up for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just make clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no -- can I make it absolutely clear we were perfectly well aware that what we had identified was Rule 68 in that interview we merely asked -- our shortcoming was that we failed to disclose it in a timely fashion but Mr. Ackerman is now saying something different. But Your Honour, as I say, rather than go round the houses on this, if we can be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The intention is this, after all you referred this matter to the Chamber because you were yourself not exactly -- you didn't want to take the risk of saying there is no -- so this is why we went into the matter. We have identified certain points that we think are Rule 68. And that you should disclose. We will go into as much detail as we think is necessary for the purpose of the written decision and that will be it. But to if we have the help of the full transcripts that would make our life easier because it puts everything in quotes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour may only -- I'll see if we can arrange that tomorrow although it's a holiday, because otherwise you wouldn't get it until Monday which may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can have it tomorrow it will be much better because then if we are not sitting on Monday we can work with it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As much that I will be coming into work tomorrow nobody else will be or very few people will be because it's a holiday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be here tomorrow, Ms. Korner. So anything else you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can I just mention, I mentioned it to Mr. Ackerman just so Your Honours are aware, because of the vast amount of translation that had to be done, in particular in respect of military court records, the translations that we had done are not authorised translations. And we've asked Mr. Ackerman to consider whether he requires them to be sent in for revision and authorised or if we can just leave the translations that we have subject to if there is anything that they think is clearly wrong then we'll have it sent in for proper translation, I'm just alerting Your Honours to if it comes up in one of the next witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we live up with that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I told Ms. Korner that we are going to look into that and see if we can get by with that. We probably can but I don't want to say we can until we get a chance to look at them and see what condition they are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather you come to some sort of conclusion because if you do not accept that -- that we -- going forward, then of course, Ms. Korner requires time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will do that as promptly as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind you of Rule 94 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm getting ready to talk to you about that. I have almost completed the Prijedor Rule 92 bis transcripts I have been reading transcripts the last several days non-stop. I'm halfway through the last one which is the biggest one then I'll start reading the Rule 94 transcripts and right behind those are the Bosanski Novi 92 bis issues that are now in a motion that's been filed and we may be moving at a pace that Ms. Korner seems is slow but it certainly is faster than I can keep up with and I seem to be getting further behind every day but I read transcripts until my eyes glaze over and then I wait a while and then I read some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, it was my intention to have it on record that we do think that you have proceeded with the Rule 92 bis process very efficiently. We are quite happy with what you have provided us so far by way of response. Which enables my staff, we discussed it this morning, enables my safe to hand down a decision pretty soon which would help the Prosecution in turn prepare adequately ahead. We have sufficient information from the Defence in that respect, and we should be able to work with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there are two left. One I made an inquiry of Ms. Korner about and I think they are accepting a suggestion that I made in that regard so I can give you my answer on that one. And the other one I've got this much transcript left to read and then I'll be able to do that one. So I suppose by tonight that the final motion the final response will be filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Ackerman. Any -- anything else? I thank you. And we will meet again, please God, on Friday morning we are sitting, no? Are we sitting in the morning on Friday? Yes. No. Yes, yes, yes. We are sitting in the morning, yes. 9.00 in this same courtroom. Courtroom II. So I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next week we are afternoons. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next week we are afternoons, yes. Let me check. We are definitely 12th and 13th I think we are definitely in the morning, 12th and 13th. The other days, I think 9th, 10th, 11th, we are indeed in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me appeal to you not to do anything with the 11th because I have an important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, except the 11th we are sitting in the morning, Monday and Tuesday we are sitting in the afternoon. Wednesday, 11th, we are sitting in the morning in Courtroom III but then if you are directly -- I know that you are involved but if you are directly involved in it, there is the Appeals Chamber interlocutory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 10th is the day I'm concerned about. If we are sitting in the afternoon of the 10th, I don't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sitting in the morning on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sitting on the morning of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 10th we are sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right that's all I care about. And I don't care about the Appeal Decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just mentioned it just in case it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Korner or either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We'll meet on Friday.
